title: Meta announces camera-free glasses, dedicated Muse AI gadget, more
snippet: Meta announced today a series of AI-powered devices, including the Muse Charm, a palm-sized gadget designed specifically for its new Muse AI assistant. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Meta announced today a series of AI-powered devices, including the Muse Charm, a palm-sized gadget designed specifically for its new Muse AI assistant. Here are the details.

Meta kicked off its Meta Connect 2026 event today, its yearly showcase for new AI technologies, wearables, and VR products.

Last year, the biggest announcement was the Meta Ray-Ban Display, the company’s first smart glasses with a built-in display that can show messages, navigation, Meta AI responses, and more.

At the time, Meta’s AI-powered glasses lineup was already gaining significant traction, with Meta and EssilorLuxottica going on to sell more than 7 million units for the year.

Since then, Meta’s camera-equipped glasses have faced growing scrutiny over privacy and ethics, as there has been no shortage of discussions involving privacy, ethics, and the general pushback on AI.

Today, Meta announced the Ray-Ban Meta Audio, its first pair of camera-free smart glasses, which starts at $349 and will be available beginning October 13.

The Ray-Ban Meta Audio retains features such as music and podcast playback, calls, and live translation, offering many of the same audio features as Meta’s camera-equipped glasses. They also support Muse, Meta’s recently launched personal AI agent.

That said, Meta also announced the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) tonight, featuring a slimmer design, up to nine hours of battery life, and a new action button, while retaining the 12MP camera and 3K video recording introduced with the previous generation.

The new action button can be customized in the Meta AI app to provide one-touch access to Meta AI or other features, such as live translation. The Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today, starting at $449.

In tonight’s event, the company also announced the Meta VR Glasses, a roughly 100-gram VR headset designed to look and feel more like a pair of glasses. The device features what Meta calls a “5K Infinite Display built on micro-OLED panels,” built-in Meta AI, eye and hand tracking, and a separate pocketable puck that handles processing, battery, and storage.

Meta is pitching the VR Glasses as a personal cinema, gaming device, and workspace. They are also the first IMAX Enhanced-certified VR device, with support for 3D movies and immersive live sports.

Alongside the Meta VR Glasses, the company also introduced a new hologram feature that can create a photorealistic avatar that reflects a user’s real-time expressions and reactions during video calls.

Meta says that a version of the feature is also coming to Meta Ray-Ban Display, where users can create a digital version of their face for hands-free video calls, beginning with WhatsApp.

The Meta VR Glasses will go on sale in spring 2027 for $1,299.99.

Rounding up tonight’s glassware news, Meta also expanded its own Meta Glasses lineup with two new styles, Capri and Nova, a new collection designed with LISA, and the $249 Meta Adventurer, its most affordable pair of smart glasses yet.

The company also introduced a limited-edition Meta Fury model and a new Ivory colorway for its Kylie Jenner collaboration.

At tonight’s event, Meta also announced the Muse Charm, a palm-sized device built specifically around its recently launched Muse personal AI agent. Meta launched Muse earlier this month, and the app has since risen to the No. 1 spot on both the U.S. App Store and Google Play.

According to Bloomberg, the Muse Charm was developed by Meta’s new design lab, led by former Apple interface design chief Alan Dye, alongside the company’s Superintelligence AI group.

The Muse Charm, which Meta refers to as a “holdable,” features a roughly 2-inch OLED touchscreen with a customizable Muse character at the center of the interface. Users can change its appearance, outfits, voice, and other attributes, and interact with Muse directly through the device.

The device also includes front- and rear-facing cameras, speakers, microphones, 5G connectivity, and a USB-C port. The cameras can capture photos and videos, but Bloomberg reports they are primarily intended to provide Muse with visual context for analysis and AI-assisted actions, rather than to serve as traditional cameras.

Users set up and sync the Charm through the Muse app on iPhone or Android. Two Charm devices can also recognize and interact with each other when placed nearby.

Meta plans to begin selling the Muse Charm in December. The company has not yet announced a price, but Bloomberg reports that it is expected to cost roughly as much as a smartwatch.

What do you make of Meta’s announcements? Let us know in the comments.

title: Report: AI glasses shipments surged 263% in H1 2026 as Apple prepares to enter the market
snippet: Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Counterpoint Research says global AI glasses shipments surged 263% during the first half of 2026, with Meta comfortably leading the display-less segment amid growing privacy concerns. Here are the details.

While Meta’s first-generation smart glasses, launched with Ray-Ban, failed to gain much traction, its second-generation devices have been far more successful.

Earlier this year, Francesco Milleri, CEO of Ray-Ban owner EssilorLuxottica, said the two companies had sold more than 7 million AI glasses in 2025, putting a 10-million annual sales target within reach for the end of 2026.

Throughout the last year, Meta has largely had the display-less AI glasses market to itself, while most major rivals are still developing their own hardware.

Apple, for instance, is rumored to be developing its own display-less smart glasses to compete with Meta’s Ray-Bans, with a launch currently targeted for 2027. The glasses are expected to rely heavily on Siri and Apple Intelligence, with cameras, microphones, and speakers built into the frame, while a more advanced version with an AR display is reportedly still several years away.

In recent months, however, Meta’s camera-equipped smart glasses have faced increasing scrutiny, with the “perv glasses” label gaining traction as reports of non-consensual filming and harassment have drawn wider attention⁠.

That said, Counterpoint Research says Meta still accounted for 94% of global display-less AI glasses shipments in the first half of 2026, with its volumes growing 260% year over year. Xiaomi and Alibaba came in at 1% each, with other brands accounting for the remaining 4%.

North America reportedly accounted for 50% of total shipments of display-less AI glasses, with Western Europe accounting for 28%, Australia for 4.4%, followed by the Asia-Pacific region with 4%, Latin America with 3.8%, India with 3.7%, China with 3%, and the UAE with 2%.

Here’s Counterpoint on how it sees this market going forward:

“Despite near-term challenges, we expect the AI glasses market to maintain its strong growth trajectory as Meta, Google, Samsung and Apple intensify their investments and competition. The next phase of growth will be driven by agentic AI glasses offering more proactive, context-aware experiences, enabled by advancements in agent-integrated software, operating systems, voice interaction, and ultra-low-power sensing and computing technologies. These developments are expected to create new growth opportunities for component vendors in the AI glasses ecosystem. We also expect a wider range of AI glasses form factors to emerge to address privacy concerns associated with cameras, including camera-free AI audio glasses and AI glasses equipped with cameras primarily for contextual understanding rather than photo or video capture.”

Counterpoint’s report also detailed the AR & AI glasses segment, which they define as “AI glasses equipped with the necessary display(s) and optical components to enable an optical see-through experience.”

According to the report, shipments in this segment surged 449% year over year, with Rokid accounting for 41% of the market, followed by Meta at 37%, Even Realities at 11%, Alibaba at 7%, INMO at 2%, and other brands collectively accounting for the remaining 2%.

Region-wise, China accounted for 45% of total shipments in this market, followed by North America at 41% and the rest of the world at 14%.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro series goes official with ‘privacy screen,’ 8,500 mAh battery, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6
snippet: Xiaomi has just launched its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in China with flagship specs, massive batteries, and a pair of 200MP cameras too. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi has just launched its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max in China with flagship specs, massive batteries, and a pair of 200MP cameras too.

With a global launch to come later, Xiaomi has unveiled its new Xiaomi 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Both devices run on the latest Snapdragon chips and carry over features from last year, such as the rear-facing display. 

The big new feature here is a “privacy screen,” Xiaomi’s implementation of the Privacy Display from Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra. Xiaomi immediately one-ups Samsung by putting the tech on both its top-end and compact flagship releases, while also supporting the feature more flexibly in its software. This also includes a feature that uses the front-facing camera to detect onlookers and activate the privacy screen automatically, as well as location-based triggers so it can turn on in crowded public areas without you needing to manually activate it, as The Verge points out.

The rest of the spec sheet is strong, with solid-looking displays on both devices, huge batteries, and Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 in both devices – the Pro Max getting the “Extreme” variant. Visually, both phones look identical, though the Pro Max gets a crazy-looking transparent edition.

	

Xiaomi 18 Pro

6.4-inch, 2436×1120 120Hz AMOLED front display

2.7-inch, 912×596 120Hz rear display

7,000 mAh battery

100W wired/27W wireless charging

200MP main camera, 200MP 3.2x telephoto, 50MP 102-degree ultrawide

Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6

12/16GB RAM, 256/512/1TB UFS 4.1 storage

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max

6.9-inch, 2624×1208 120Hz AMOLED front display

2.9-inch, 976×596 120Hz rear display

8,500 mAh battery

100W wired/27W wireless charging

200MP main camera, 200MP 3.2x telephoto, 50MP 102-degree ultrawide

Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6

12/16GB RAM, 256/512/1TB UFS 4.1 storage

Xiaomi’s 18 Pro series starts at 5,999CNY, just shy of $900 USD, but international pricing remains to be seen. The Xiaomi 17 launched internationally in February 2026, so we can probably expect a similar timeline this time, but Xiaomi has confirmed the Pro models will debut outside of China this time, unlike the Xiaomi 17 Pro.

title: Enveda secures $311M to bring more nature-derived AI drugs into clinical trials
snippet: The round valued the AI biotech at $2 billion. It is currently testing drugs that treat skin conditions and preserve weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.
fullText:
Enveda, a biotech startup that uses AI to discover new drugs in the natural world, has raised a $311 million Series E at a $2 billion valuation. The fresh funding, which was led by Catalio Capital Management, with participation from Iconiq and others, doubles the valuation Enveda achieved 12 months ago.

The idea behind Enveda is that powerful medicines could be harnessed from plants and microbes, rather than synthesized from scratch in a lab. Viswa Colluru, an early employee of Recursion Pharmaceuticals, founded Enveda in 2019 to speed up the process of discovering these new drugs using AI and other techniques.

While AI hasn’t yet produced any FDA-approved drugs, Enveda is among the wave of companies advancing AI-discovered candidates into human clinical trials. The startup is currently testing several drugs in patients, including one targeting severe skin conditions and another designed to help maintain weight loss after stopping GLP-1s.

title: The old cybersecurity model is breaking
snippet: As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even seeing companies like Instinct and Simile bring in nine-figure checks and valuations that wouldn’t have made sense a […]
fullText:
Loading the player…

As concern over AI safety and rogue agents continue to make headlines, it’s no surprise that cybersecurity stocks are rising, or that investors are pouring massive amounts of capital into startups trying to build the next generation of security for an AI-native world. We’re even seeing companies like Instinct and Simile bring in nine-figure checks and valuations that wouldn’t have made sense a few years ago. 

With a front row seat to it all is Shardul Shah, a partner at Index Ventures who’s spent nearly two decades investing in cybersecurity and enterprise software — including six consecutive rounds in cloud security startup Wiz, which Google acquired for $32 billion earlier this year in one of its largest acquisitions ever. 

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Shah joins Rebecca Bellan to break down why he thinks periodic, human-in-the-loop security can’t keep up anymore, and why Index continues investing in AI-native security companies at stages that once required much more proof.

title: Xiaomi 18 Pro has a Privacy Display that does more than Galaxy S26 Ultra, launches this week [Video]
snippet: Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi has confirmed support for the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display on the upcoming Xiaomi 18 Pro, and it apparently does a lot more than Samsung’s implementation of the feature.

The Privacy Display on Galaxy S26 Ultra is a hardware feature that can help hide the contents of your display from onlookers by physically altering how the light of the display shines outward. It’s a very clever feature which, despite some trade-offs, has been very well-received.

Now, it’s coming to a Xiaomi flagship.

In a teaser posted to Weibo, Xiaomi confirms that the Xiaomi 18 Pro will ship with a “smart privacy screen” that looks virtually identical to the Galaxy S26 Ultra’s Privacy Display. When activated, content is obfuscated at an angle, only allowing you as the person looking at the display straight-on to clearly see everything.

	

Similar to Samsung, Xiaomi looks to be allowing this to work in specific apps or on only certain parts of the display, like a notification, instead of being an all-or-nothing option. 

Notably, though, Xiaomi also shows the feature working on a floating app window, in split screen, and even on specific notifications on the lockscreen. While Samsung is working on improvements, Xiaomi seems to be delivering quite a bit more versatility right out of the gate.

You can see everything in action in the video below:

Xiaomi 18 Pro is officially set to debut on September 23 – just two days from now – with some key details already confirmed (via GSMArena) including battery sizes up to 8,500 mAh, another rear-facing display, and more.

title: So Many New Meta Glasses: Muse AI Everywhere, and Ray-Bans Without a Camera
snippet: At Meta Connect, I tried out the AI agent, hearing enhancement and other features on all the new glasses. I was also disappointed at how little’s been done on the privacy front.
fullText:
I talked to “Henry,” a Muse agent in my AI glasses, as I stared at a box of Kind bars. Henry was trained as if it were the assistant to a 38-year-old bodybuilding marketing executive. Henry told me whether I should eat Kind bars and also helped me plan my workout schedule. 

This was me getting a preview of Muse, Meta’s AI agent that’s already on phones and Macs, but this time it was on Meta’s AI glasses. If you were concerned about AI on what many people are calling “pervert glasses” before, they’re about to get supercharged very soon.

But I also tried on a camera-free pair of Meta glasses that gave me audio assistance, meaning privacy-invading, pervy images aren’t an issue.

This was at Meta’s Connect developer conference this week, where the focus was on AI, VR and glasses and where Meta fired out a whole bunch of updates and many new designs. It was also getting a jump on the launch of Google and Samsung’s own AI glasses, which are just around the corner. 

Some of Meta’s new glasses designs come with better battery life, some with added hearing assistance, and some, made by Thai rap star and actor Lisa, come with collectible charms. But amid all of this, there was very little about fundamental changes that would address the privacy concerns and fears surrounding a wearable category that so many companies are diving into.

Every time I wear or talk about smart glasses, people increasingly give me side eye. This has been a very bad summer for global opinions on AI-enabled and camera-equipped glasses, a category in which Meta is a leader. But with Google, Samsung and a ton of others – including Apple – expected to enter the fray next year, it’s going to get crowded and weird fast. Meta’s answer to all of this: more glasses, more features, including literally getting in our faces with its new agentic AI tool, Muse.

There is a new FDA-cleared hearing enhancement mode in Meta’s glasses that I tried, which costs $149 to activate. There are new Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses with slightly better battery life, and camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses with even better battery life (up to 12 hours). 

Muse could be the biggest news of all, especially as Meta goes head-to-head against Google and Samsung’s Gemini-infused wearables. But I was also surprised that no new fitness features were announced after Meta’s push into the space with Oakley-branded visors last year, and Meta’s prescription-challenged Ray-Ban Displays, while becoming available to order in more countries, have barely changed at all.

So, let’s break it all down. I’m still trying to digest it myself.

I tried Muse on Meta’s glasses at a single demo on Meta’s campus.Scott Stein/CNET

Meta’s putting its Muse AI agent on its glasses

Muse is an agentic AI system that’s been well-received by some early reviewers and in-app downloads since it emerged just a couple of weeks ago. Its appearance on Meta’s glasses now seems inevitable, especially since the faster-responding Muse Spark AI model has given them a performance boost. 

The only chance I got to try Muse on glasses was a very quick and pretty canned demo, and the arrival timing for Muse on glasses is still unclear. Also unclear is exactly how capable Muse will truly be or how safe. The agentic AI can already tap into personal accounts of all sorts if you let it, and it can buy things for you or manage your data, but it doesn’t promise encryption or privacy. That’s why I’ve avoided connecting it to anything in my own life, and not all accounts will allow hook-ins: Amazon just blocked Muse from enabling shopping on its sites.

My Muse glasses demo showed very little of meaningful, deeper agent hooks to data I’d recognize, since it wasn’t my own being accessed. I did notice that Muse took a while to complete some actions when rescheduling workouts for the marketing manager Muse agent Henry was set up to serve. Muse worked over audio, with no sense of progress status for completing a task.

Meta is introducing some privacy updates to how its glasses handle data, promising a new Private Processing system in the future that will run on confidential virtual machines in the cloud, a system that Meta’s using now in WhatsApp and Meta AI but plans to extend to all tools for Meta glasses. It’s not here yet, though, and it doesn’t make me feel any more convinced that any of the systems can be trusted, though, and I certainly feel lots of anxiety about handing over any agentic control of my personal data to any system.

But the space is moving fast. Google Gemini can already handle a lot of agentic actions, and Samsung and Google’s glasses will be able to do them. Apple’s new Siri, meanwhile, also has increasingly agent-like actions in its connected AI and apps. And OpenAI could be introducing more wearables with direct support for its services, too. Everyone in tech seems to want something like Iron Man’s Jarvis for your face, and few actually have it. Meta’s casting its hat in the ring.

Meta’s two Ray-Ban Audio glasses models: Clubmaster (left) and Burbank (right)Scott Stein/CNET

There are camera-free Meta Ray-Ban glasses now

One way to avoid pervert glasses concerns? Not having cameras on glasses at all. I tried out the new line of camera-free Meta Ray-Ban Audio glasses, which promise 12-hour battery life (a notable bump from 8 to 9 hours on Meta’s recent glasses). There are just two designs for now: Clubmaster, which is a new look, and the more familiar square Burbank.

There’s not a lot new with Ray-Ban Audio glasses. They’re Meta glasses, minus the camera. A programmable action button on top of one arm still activates Meta AI, and one arm still has a touch bar for volume control. The audio sounded as good to me as Meta’s other models, but the battery boost could be a welcome addition. So could the social comfort of not having a camera on glasses.

But they’re not cheap. At $379 to $479, they’re actually more expensive than Meta’s recently launched line of self-branded smart glasses. Oddly, Meta didn’t make a non-Ray-Ban “Meta” branded (and likely less expensive) pair of audio glasses. Not yet, at least.

Nothing’s much changed on the camera front, either. A new landscape mode for photos sounded promising at first, but it works via digital cropping, and I haven’t tried it yet.

The phone app dashboard for Hearing Enhancement, which I got to demo briefly at Meta.Scott Stein/CNET

FDA-cleared hearing enhancement costs extra

In a move that mirrors a growing trend in hearing tech, Meta’s adding an FDA-cleared hearing assistance mode to its glasses, called Hearing Enhancement, which runs a hearing test to tune the experience for people with mild to moderate hearing loss. Apple’s AirPods Pro earbuds launched a similar feature two years ago.

Unlike Apple’s feature, though, you have to pay to enable Meta’s extra. It’s either $149, with a 30-day free trial to test how it works first, or included with a Meta One subscription that’ll run on glasses soon.

I hate subscriptions, especially for health features. A one-time cost feels more bearable. But it also pushes the total price up for a pair of Meta glasses as potential hearing aids.

To simulate how they work, Meta put foam earbuds in my ears while activating the mode during a conversation I had with Ravish Mehra, Meta’s director of research science. That’s far from a true simulation of actual hearing loss, but I got some sense of how the mode enhanced treble and clarity in sounds and conversations, like a more refined version of Meta’s existing Conversation Focus mode. Hearing Enhancement works in a targeted beam-forming mode that attends to a person, or more ambiently.

Mehra told me that the mode, when running, works for about 4  hours on Meta’s recent glasses models, but longer on the Ray-Ban Audio glasses. The extra fee could have been avoided (as Apple did), but Mehra cited R&D costs as one reason for the upcharge. I’m curious how AirPods and Meta glasses would compare for someone who actually needs the hearing assistance, something I couldn’t vet. With glasses, at least there wouldn’t be a need for any buds in your ears.

Meta Adventurer glasses in the new Lisa design are coming soon.Scott Stein/CNET

Lisa is making a pair of Meta Glasses too

I actually didn’t know who Lisa was, but she’s a famous rapper, actor and social media star who’s making her own custom-branded pair of Meta glasses, in the spirit of the Kylie Jenner glasses Meta launched in June. (My colleague Faith Chihil, one of CNET’s social media producers, flipped out at the Lisa news.)

The Lisa glasses come with a collectible charm, one of 14 types. They’re also decorated with stars on the arms. Lisa fans and collectors might be excited by this. I’m not.

But Meta’s also releasing a bunch more frame designs and colors, including some new Meta Glasses looks. Meta says there are over 100 designs and colors across all types now, and it felt that way when I browsed a bunch of new frames at Meta’s campus.

A new Aviator line of Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 smart glasses.Scott Stein/CNET

Gen 3 Meta Ray-Bans have new designs, slightly better battery

There are also new third-gen Meta Ray-Bans, but they’re not nearly as notable as the second-gen ones I wore last year. The battery boost on third-gen models is just an hour more than with Gen 2 — 9  hours total at best. That matches the claims for Google and Samsung’s imminent smart glasses, which is likely no coincidence.

There are a few frame designs, mostly variations on familiar looks. One pops, though: an aviator design that I tried out without my prescription added. They’re bold, kinda interesting, and…I felt a bit sinister wearing them.

The third-gen glasses are also more expensive, ranging from $449 to $529 without a prescription. Meta’s self-branded glasses, released in June, start at $299 and have nearly identical features, except for that tiny battery bump.

This is actually a virtual version of me in Meta’s new Hologram avatar. I animated it by talking on Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays.Scott Stein/CNET

Meta Ray-Ban Displays haven’t evolved much at all (except for Holograms)

Last year, Meta made a big deal with its display-enabled Ray-Bans and innovative neural band interface, a setup that seemed to push toward a future where full AR glasses lurk. 

And yet, a year later, Meta has no significant improvements for Displays. They’ll be available in more countries this year, and may be easier to buy. But they still don’t work for a larger range of prescriptions, limited to just a -4 maximum. My eyes still won’t work with them.

Meta has been opening up more app development for its glasses and rolling out more features for Displays over the last year. Still, I expected Meta might find a way to blend its neural band with a smartwatch, perhaps one of Garmin’s models, since Meta and Garmin already have a partnership. But that didn’t happen either. The prices of the glasses are also still the same.

The most interesting thing about the Displays is the addition of Holograms, a hyper-realistic video chat avatar system that I tested out at Meta’s campus and was wowed by. It scans your face with a phone app and then projects your presence to the phone screen (or glasses, or VR headset) of whoever you’re calling, to surprisingly realistic effect. It’ll only be available to a limited test group at first in beta and will work on WhatsApp, but deliver the sort of simulated video chat on glasses that has been promised by Meta for years.

Besides camera-free Meta glasses (left), the design of Meta’s new glasses and camera design (right) remains the same.Scott Stein/CNET

Sorry, no watch, new fitness modes or major privacy improvements yet

Meanwhile, I was also surprised that Meta had no fitness updates at Connect, despite introducing Oakley-branded Vanguard visors last year and Garmin-connected workout features.

The Muse agent can connect to fitness and health functions, but a lack of new dedicated fitness features leaves a gap that Google might fill quickly with possibilities for Fitbit integration on its upcoming glasses, and an interconnection between WearOS watches and its glasses to act as a mini control dashboard and even preview photos. 

Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth hinted to me last year that the neural band could evolve into a watch, but those plans haven’t yet materialized. Unlike Google and Apple’s wearables, Meta’s glasses are limited in how they connect to phones, using an app and, in the future, agentic hooks via Muse’s AI. 

And also, biggest of all, Meta’s privacy issues feel barely addressed. It’s still as easy to take a photo in public as before, and nothing’s changed with how the glasses present themselves to others: They’re easy to confuse with regular glasses (to Meta’s credit, design-wise) and still just show a small LED light when recording.

And while Meta has promises of a private compute layer in the cloud for its future features, can they be trusted, and will third-party observers get access in any way? Will any of these new agentic features misfire unpredictably, as we’ve already seen with AI agents? The answer there feels like a “when” rather than an “if.” 

But Meta won’t be alone in the pursuit of agentic AI wearables. It’s just the biggest and first in the door. There’s a lot of potential lurking in wearable AI, and lots of concerns. And Meta’s continuing to roll forward through all of it.

title: The FAA Is Testing an AI-Powered Air Traffic Management Tool
snippet: No, ChatGPT will not be clearing you for takeoff.
fullText:
For years, there have been shortages of air traffic control personnel, leading to delays and congestion. To remedy these troubles, the Federal Aviation Administration and the US Department of Transportation are turning to a new tool: AI. 

On Monday, these agencies announced that they’re beginning a trial of the new system, called Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories, at three airports around the nation’s capital – Reagan National Airport, Dulles International Airport and BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport. 

This $875 million software overhaul is not a replacement for human air traffic control operators, the DOT said, but is intended to reduce pressure on personnel by predicting delays and cancellations, and providing recommendations to the humans who retain control over flight operations. 

Margaret Wallace, an assistant professor of aviation management at the Florida Institute of Technology, said meaningful action is necessary to address the aging air traffic control infrastructure, and calls to modernize the system have been ongoing – yet unanswered – for years. 

While SMART is an important first step, she says, it “does not eliminate the human element,” and controllers need to remain at the forefront of every stage of implementation. 

“If implemented carefully, however, the technology behind this initiative has the potential to begin a significant transformation in the efficiency and modernization of the US air traffic system,” Wallace said in an email. 

How the SMART system works

It may be alarming to read “artificial intelligence” and “air traffic management” in the same sentence. So let’s unpack what this system actually is before deciding to never get on another flight again. 

Each day, the FAA manages close to 45,000 flights in the US. Even slight delays, changes in weather conditions, and reroutes can lead to airspace congestion and overcapacity. SMART was designed to centralize 200 data streams of flight paths, wind, weather, staffing metrics and more into one platform for a comprehensive overview of what’s happening in the sky and on the ground at airports for better management of these flights.  

From this consolidated data, human controllers can “anticipate demand, weather and airspace constraints and plan hours, days and even weeks ahead,” according to the press release. 

The US DOT says these measures are to upgrade “the FAA from a reactive approach to a predictive one.”

“By fundamentally reshaping how we manage our airspace and preventing problems before they happen, SMART will slash those frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers and lower travel prices,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement.

Will it actually help? It’s too early to tell, and the union representing air traffic controllers said it was not involved in the program’s development. 

The National Air Traffic Controllers Association said in a statement it “believes any new technology should complement and not replace the experience, training and professional judgment of air traffic controllers who are responsible for the safety of the National Airspace System.”

The system was built by a company called Air Space Intelligence, an aerospace and defense AI company based in the US that has already partnered with the US Air Force, major US airlines (Alaska Airlines, Delta Air Lines and United Airlines) and the Department of Defense. 

In the press release announcing the rollout of the air traffic management system, CEOs from top airlines, including United, Delta, American and Southwest, expressed encouragement over the initiative. 

Still, air traffic experts emphasize the importance of remaining cautious as this new system rolls out. 

“My biggest initial concern is controller training and human-factors integration,” Wallace said. “That is not necessarily a criticism of this particular system; it is a challenge that comes with introducing any significant new technology into a complex, safety-critical environment.

“FAA leadership will need to ensure that implementation and testing are deliberate, that controllers receive adequate training and that appropriate safeguards remain in place throughout the transition,” she said.

The FAA plans to gradually expand SMART to other airports across the country. 

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Macy Meyer

This includes writing about consumer AI products and their real-world impact, from breakthrough tools reshaping daily life to the intimate ways people interact with AI technology day-to-day. title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
snippet: Meta says the camera-free glasses will be lighter and have up to 12 hours battery life.
fullText:
Confirming earlier reports, Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse.

The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349.

While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people, often men, were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained.

This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. 

“Once you get used to high quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses.

Image Credits:Meta/Screenshot /

Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. 

They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed.

The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted.

Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life.

The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also be roll out to more countries globally, Meta said.

All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. 

The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data.

snippet: Sam Altman attends a UN Security Council meeting on AI. | Getty Images OpenAI's artificial intelligence agents hacked an Australian government website and attempted to breach numerous other government and university websites. The attack appears to be the first confirmed instance of a rogue AI agent breaching a government website, adding fuel to rapidly intensifying concerns about the safety of advanced AI systems and the responsibility of the companies building them. Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an agent from the American AI lab "infiltrated" Australia's Medicare statistics portal and "accessed both public and non-public file … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
OpenAI’s artificial intelligence agents hacked an Australian government website and attempted to breach numerous other government and university websites. The attack appears to be the first confirmed instance of a rogue AI agent breaching a government website, adding fuel to rapidly intensifying concerns about the safety of advanced AI systems and the responsibility of the companies building them.

Speaking on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an agent from the American AI lab “infiltrated” Australia’s Medicare statistics portal and “accessed both public and non-public files.” Medicare is Australia’s universal health insurance program.

Albanese said personal information does not appear to have been accessed in the breach and that there is no evidence of a broader compromise to the network, but noted “investigations are ongoing.”

“This situation is obviously unacceptable,” Albanese said, adding that he had spoken with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman “to express Australia’s extreme concern.” Despite the breach happening in June, Albanese said the tech giant only notified the government about the incident earlier this month and did so via an email to a generic “public mailbox.”

Unlike previous agent incidents, which largely involved systems being tested for their cybersecurity skills, these latest hacks were the result of a more pedestrian task — data collection — going wrong. In a statement to The Verge, OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines said the models were attempting to “look up answers” during an internal evaluation. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.”

The timeline of the incident and its disclosure is likely to prove particularly inflammatory in the discussions of corporate behavior and transparency that follow. Albanese stressed the delay in disclosure is particularly unacceptable. OpenAI told the BBC in an unattributed statement that it did not become aware until August, when reviewing misaligned model activity.

OpenAI spokesperson Oscar Haines told The Verge the company’s “review found no evidence of patient records being accessed,” and that “the information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.” Haines said OpenAI has notified the relevant organizations and is providing technical information to support their investigations and address potential security vulnerabilities. “Our overall review is ongoing, and we remain committed to transparency about these issues and to sharing what we learn as that work continues,” Haines said.

Three further incidents of rogue AI activity linked to OpenAI agents were also reported on Wednesday by research lab Transluce. The group, which describes itself as a “nonprofit research lab dedicated to public oversight” of AI, said it had identified evidence that OpenAI’s systems had attempted to compromise websites linked to the University of New Mexico, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, and Data USA, a non-government platform that aggregates data from US government sources. It said the last two of these were directly linked to an agent swarm OpenAI has previously admitted originated from them.

Haines confirmed the incidents in a statement to The Verge and said the company had reached out to those involved. “Our initial review suggests that much of the activity described in Transluce’s report overlaps with cases at varying stages of investigation in our ongoing review of misaligned model activity,” he said. “In our broader review, we’re continuing to prioritize the most serious incidents while expanding our work to lower-severity activity, including agents spamming websites. Given the scale of this work and the need to verify each case, we expect the review to take months.”

OpenAI’s handling of the Australian Medicare incident is certain to place notions of corporate responsibility at the center of future discussions surrounding AI, which are often obscured with the language used to describe such attacks. OpenAI has already faced allegations of obfuscation for not disclosing similar unsanctioned activity by its agents, and efforts to prioritize investigating what it deems the most serious incidents raise the obvious question of what basis it uses to make such assessments, and how much has yet to be revealed. It echoes similar questions recently raised about Google, which did not disclose real-world attacks from its own agents.

The newly-revealed breaches come amid mounting concerns about the safety of advanced AI and the reliability of the companies developing it, largely ignited by the coordinated attack OpenAI agents launched on Hugging Face earlier this year. Worries over safety have led industry insiders to call for slowing down the pace of AI development and the global nature of the incidents has sparked significant debate among nations about how to implement stronger safeguards. Eyes will largely remain on the US and China, however, as these are the only two countries operating at the very frontier of the technology. Both appear to be resisting calls to slow down, and seem locked in a race to build the most advanced AI. Leaders from the two countries are set to meet on Thursday.

title: Discord Introduces Alternative Age Verification Tools After Pushback
snippet: Teenage users have options, but some appear safer than others. We pick the best options.
fullText:
After Discord users pushed back on ID requirements for age verification, the social platform announced in a blog post on Tuesday that it would implement age verification for teens — but not in the way people expected.

“Discord is introducing a new approach to age assurance, strengthening teen safety without requiring everyone to prove their age,” the company said in an email to CNET. “More than 90% of users won’t be asked to confirm their age. Most will either be placed into an age group automatically or will be able to continue using Discord without confirming their age unless they want to access age-restricted content, spaces, or settings.”

For those who do need to verify, Discord focuses on measuring “age signals” for teens rather than actual IDs, and it tells users it will not receive any direct data about them except their age signal results. The platform will work with a variety of vendors who will examine different types of data to assess a person’s age. Discord says those vendors won’t use any of this data for ad targeting or AI model training.

This follows a Discord-related data breach in 2025, which exposed 70,000 government ID photos of users, among with other information, on a vendor website.

The good news is that young Discord users can now choose how to verify their age, including options that don’t show their faces or IDs. Some of Discord’s options look fairly privacy-friendly, such as the ability to use documentation already in Google Wallet or the Apple App Store to verify age. If you’ve been using Apple’s store long enough, you may not have to send any further documentation at all. They can also use a site called AgeKey to create a reusable age credential. This allows teens to verify their age across multiple platforms without sharing their personal data directly with Discord.

Some troubling choices

However, some of Discord’s verification options raise serious privacy concerns.

“While estimating age based on user behavior is less invasive than requiring users to upload photos, credit card information or a state-issued ID, age-gating the internet creates dangerous new forms of surveillance, censorship, and exclusion,” Electronic Frontier Foundation senior counsel David Greene told CNET.

Discord includes a facial age-estimation option that requires a video selfie. Although the site says all facial analysis happens locally on the device, this use of AI still gives us pause. Experts point to ongoing accuracy challenges and inherent data risks, raising concerns over how corporate policies and algorithmic parameters might evolve in the future.

We’re also not fans of the credit-card check option, which not only costs money but sends credit card details to a third party, which may increase financial security risks.

Inaccurate age estimates can always happen, and they complicate the process. While Discord notes that users can initially switch to alternative confirmation methods, manual review serves as the fallback if those options fail. However, this manual route is a last resort and requires a human representative to personally verify both a government ID and a photograph.

title: Meta’s Muse AI Agent Has Been Downloaded Half a Million Times — With a Serious Bug
snippet: The security flaw has been patched, but there are plenty of reasons to hesitate about giving AI too much access.
fullText:
If you’ve seen a cartoonish character at the top of your Instagram feed lately, that’s Muse. Meta’s newest AI agent, or bot, wants to be your digital assistant. But Meta had to rush to patch a serious zero-day bug in Muse’s code this week, highlighting just how treacherous it can be to hand over the keys to your digital life to agentic AI.

Patrick Wardle, founder of the cybersecurity firm Objective-See, was the first to spot the zero-day bug. He outlined the vulnerability in X posts, showing how a bad actor could trick the AI agent into sending a person’s Muse dictations, or audio captures, and access tokens to their own malicious server, not Meta’s servers. Wardle has a long history of finding bugs in Meta’s software.

	

			

The head of Meta’s Superintelligence Labs, David Singleton, replied to Wardle’s X post on Tuesday to confirm the company has patched the vulnerability. He added that the bug required malware to already be on a user’s computer for the exploit to work; Wardle disagrees, saying it is possible for a hacker to exploit this flaw remotely.

To prevent your Muse AI agent from being hacked, update your MacOS Muse app right now. This will ensure you’re running the latest version of the program, including the new security fix. No additional action is needed from you.

A one-off bug or persistent pattern?

Singleton wrote of the incident: “We strive to be extremely transparent about privacy and security in Muse as we know this is important to maintain your trust.” We absolutely need tech companies to be transparent, but there is still a lot unknown about AI agents like Muse.

At first glance, Muse has had a successful entrance into an already crowded field of AI agents, including those from OpenAI, SpaceXAI and Anthropic. The MacOS app was downloaded more than half a million times during its first week, according to internal data seen by The Information, making it one of the more popular AI agent choices. But to get the most value out of your AI agent, you need to grant it permission to access a lot of different things. To have Muse make you a dinner reservation, for example, it needs to be able to use your computer, access the web and potentially use your credit card info to hold the table. 

Privacy and security concerns are two of the most serious concerns with generative AI. No tech company has fully addressed all the various harms that will come from AI, be it cybersecurity hacks or losing control over our personal information used by the AI. But Meta has a longer track record than most AI startups, and its history isn’t the most reassuring. Just consider the 2016 Cambridge Analytica scandal that revealed millions of Facebook users’ data had been used improperly, or its more recent court battle and settlement over failing to protect children online.

These security reports come ahead of Wednesday’s Meta Connect, where CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to show us more about how the company is thinking about AI and AI hardware. Meta Connect has traditionally focused on Meta’s smart glasses, but rising public backlash has cast a lot of doubt on the long-term viability of the devices, sometimes dubbed “pervert glasses” due to their recording capabilities.

If Meta is going to continue down the agentic AI path, tech users need to be able to trust the company to build it responsibly. But the public’s faith in AI companies has dwindled in recent days, thanks to AI researchers airing concerns that the technology could lead to the extinction of humanity.

							Reporter 2

Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. title: Eight Sleep Launches Pod 6 With Smaller Hub and Cheaper Entry Price
snippet: The sleep tech company launched the smallest Pod of its lineup yet and introduced new sizes.
fullText:
Eight Sleep, a sleep tech company, launched the Pod 6 bed-cooling system on Wednesday with meaningful hardware changes, including a hub that’s half the size of its predecessor, new solo-size configurations and a $1,999 starting price for the solo sizes — the lowest the company has offered. The entry price for standard sizes will be $2,699.

“We redesigned the hub, so it is 50% shorter than Pod 5, while increasing thermal power. That requires a more efficient approach to the system’s internal architecture, thermal management, fluid movement and overall packaging,” Matteo Franceschetti, CEO and co-founder of Eight Sleep, told CNET. The smaller hub can slide under most standard bed frames.

For the first time since the Pod launched in 2019, customers can choose solo-size options like twin XL and half sizes for queen, king and California king. Until now, the Pod has been built for couples with standard mattress sizes. 

“For six generations, the Pod’s dual-zone design has been extremely valuable for couples, because each person can independently control their temperature and receive their own sleep data. But there are many people who want that same experience for just one side of the bed, or in a bedroom with a twin XL or split-mattress configuration,” Franceschetti said.

The Pod 6 has nine times more sensors per side and AI-powered tracking for more accurate sleep insights. The redesigned hub delivers 40% to 50% more thermal power for faster temperature response. 

Eight Sleep

Franceschetti said that the main advantage of having more sensors is improved precision and consistent tracking across different sleep positions. “People move throughout the night, and a higher density of sensors gives the system more opportunities to maintain a reliable signal, whether someone is on their back, side or shifting position.”

With these updates, the Pod 6 aims to make advanced sleep technology more accessible and versatile for individual sleepers and couples alike.

title: Five ways that the new Siri AI is frustrating iPhone and Apple Watch users
snippet: The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases. The new Siri is much better at answering questions with access to rich knowledge, can search through your messages and notes for personal context queries, and can take action based on what is on your screen with onscreen awareness. However, the new Siri is not being welcomed with open arms by everyone … more…
fullText:
The new version of Siri, Siri AI, launched to the masses this month as part of iOS 27. The new Siri is rolling out gradually to users via a waitlist, and is labelled as a ‘beta’ indicating that Apple still has some work to do in follow-up releases.

The new Siri is much better at answering questions with access to rich knowledge, can search through your messages and notes for personal context queries, and can take action based on what is on your screen with onscreen awareness. However, the new Siri is not being welcomed with open arms by everyone …

Based on social media posts, there are a few reasons why the new Siri is disappointing users. Some expect it to be able to perform tasks that Apple simply never promised would be possible, while others note they are hitting performance and reliability bugs that make using the assistant on a regular basis a frustrating affair. 

Here’s the five main categories of complaints we’ve seen from people trying Siri AI so far:

Network connectivity issues 

Some users trying out new Siri repeatedly see a “Sorry, something went wrong” error when invoking it. This appears to be caused by some kind of network communication issue between the phone and the Siri cloud backend, potentially solved by disabling a VPN or changing Wi-Fi network settings. 

However, the Siri interface does not tell the user exactly what the problem is, so they are left stuck with a ‘useless’ voice assistant. We also suspect the Apple cloud infrastructure is experiencing some intermittent downtime, which can also cause requests to fail.

Indexing problems: new Siri cannot always find things that old Siri could 

While new Siri is meant to be much better at finding things on your device, some users are finding the opposite to be the case. When asking something like “Add eggs to my grocery list in Reminders”, Siri will say it cannot find the list. We have seen repeated cases of people trying to use new Siri to turn off all their alarms, only for it to answer to say the user has no alarms. Others report that their HomeKit accessories cannot be found consistently by name.

These issues are seemingly related to underlying search indexing bugs, but it’s unclear if there are steps user can follow to remedy the situation. Some Apple Watch users even hit extremely odd cases like ‘I can’t set a timer because the Clock app isn’t installed on this device’.

Requires iPhone to be unlocked to answer requests

New Siri seems to require the device be unlocked for many requests, even if the ‘allow Siri when locked’ toggle is turned on in Settings. This applies to all sorts of queries, which old Siri never required the device to be unlocked for. Naturally, many people often try to invoke Siri in situations where the phone is locked, like in a car or on the go with AirPods. 

It seems like whenever new Siri tries to access the semantic index to garner personal context, it fails if the phone is locked. But this makes even simple commands like ‘Send message to [person name]’ more annoying, when old Siri did not have such a requirement.

Slow to respond to queries, especially on Apple Watch

Another common refrain is that new Siri is just slower to answer for them. Although on-device models play a role in how new Siri operates, much of its processing happens on the cloud with Private Cloud Compute, and a slow network connection therefore makes new Siri slow to respond, even for basic requests like sending messages or checking notifications. 

The speed complaints are especially true when using Siri AI with watchOS 27 running on an Apple Watch Series 9 or later, where even saying something like ‘start a 5 minute timer’ can take many seconds to resolve, a disappointing regression as they used to be processed almost instantly. 

Missing features or unreliable commands compared to old Siri

Despite everything that new Siri can do, there are some features of old Siri that have not yet been exposed to the new Siri system. For instance, Apple documents that asking about your Health app data is not currently supported by Siri AI. People that used the ChatGPT integration can no longer prefix their command with “Use ChatGPT” to have their request directed accordingly. 

There are also some particular phrasings of commands that old Siri would understand but new Siri gets confused about. Naturally, this annoys users who have become accustomed to asking something specific on a regular basis. This is partly due to the fact that new Siri has the potential to do so much more, that some specificly-worded queries have become ambiguous compared to the much smaller scope of classic Siri.

Aside from these classes of bugs, we’ve also seen users complain about the way new Siri is presented in the user interface. This includes criticisms of the annoyingly prominent ‘Ask Siri’ buttons that have been added across the operating system, the lack of a visible transcript of what the phone heard the user said in the new Dynamic Island UI, the fact that the middle of the screen swipe-down gesture to reveal their notifications has been commandeered to show Siri & Spotlight instead, and other complaints.

As mentioned before, the new Siri is marked as a beta and this signals that more capabilities and fixes will follow in future updates. Apple has not yet disclosed a roadmap, though, apart from announcing a rollout to a handful of more languages, coming in October. 

	

In the meantime, if you are experiencing any of the sorts of issues described above, you may want to go back to classic Siri:

How to turn off Siri AI and go back to old Siri

The easiest way to disable Siri AI on your device and quickly switch back to classic Siri is to use controls in Screen Time. Open the Settings app and navigate to Screen Time -> Content & Privacy Restrictions -> Siri and change Allowed Siri version from “Siri AI (Beta)” to “Siri Classic”. 

You can then go back to this menu later and toggle it back if you want to try Siri AI again. 

If you don’t want to use Screen Time, you can also go into Siri settings directly and turn off Siri altogether. When you re-enable it, you should be able to choose between enabling Siri Classic or Siri AI.

title: OpenAI upgrading ChatGPT and Codex with two more GPT-6 models
snippet: Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models. more…
fullText:
Earlier this month, OpenAI released the first GPT-6 model with Astra. Now GPT-6 is expanding with new GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna models.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are now available

Per the ChatGPT desktop app release notes, GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna will use fewer tokens to run than GPT-5.6 versions of the same class model.

GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna are rolling out to Codex and ChatGPT Work at lower token prices than their GPT-5.6 predecessors. Use Sol for complex coding and agentic workflows, and Luna for focused, high-volume tasks.

Both models are rolling out to Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access Luna in the desktop app. Availability depends on rollout and workspace settings; Enterprise administrators must enable the new models. In ChatGPT, the models are available in Work and Codex, but not Chat.

Note the absence of a GPT-6 Terra model. It’s expected that OpenAI is dropping the medium model in favor of just three: Terra (small), Sol (large), and Astra (extra large).

GPT-6 Sol and Luna are out. Not only are they a very significant improvement across the board, but also in writing and general "you know when you try it" quality. 

We are also permanently reducing the API price by 50% making both of them viable for a ton of new usecases and… https://t.co/vbyUhVlKH3

— Tibo (@thsottiaux) September 22, 2026

Here’s the official announcement from OpenAI:

While the most demanding and important projects still call for Astra’s full depth, work happens at different scales, rhythms, and budgets.

That’s why we’re expanding the GPT‑6 universe with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna. GPT‑6 Astra introduced a new generation of intelligence—these models help distribute the benefits of that intelligence by advancing the frontier on cost efficiency. We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The company describes its two newest models as more capable than the GPT-5.6 versions as well as more affordable than Astra (and the GPT-5.6 versions they replace). For instance, the GPT-6 versions of Sol and Luna are 50% cheaper than the GPT-5.6 versions.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing. Together, these improvements make advanced AI practical for more everyday tasks and applications at scale.

In terms of coding, this is what OpenAI says about its new models:

This year, coding agents have begun tackling tasks with more complexity, scope, and duration than ever before. At OpenAI, our internal usage has grown exponentially. Valued at API prices, daily token usage has exceeded $600 for the median researcher and $7,000 for researchers at the 90th percentile (Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI⁠). As coding agents take on longer and more demanding tasks, the cost of sustained use matters more. GPT‑6 Sol and Luna combine strong coding performance with lower API prices, giving developers more room to iterate and teams the confidence to be more ambitious about what they ask Codex to take on.

ChatGPT also excels at Computer Use, and these new models continue that push:

While GPT‑6 Astra remains the world’s best model for computer use, GPT‑6 Sol and Luna offer more cost-efficient performance than their predecessors. On OSWorld 2.0 offline, GPT‑6 Sol at xhigh effort achieves a similar score to Claude Opus 5 at medium effort—60.5% versus 60.3%—at approximately 80% lower cost per task. GPT‑6 Luna (max) is able to exceed GPT‑5.6 Sol (medium) at one tenth of its cost.

In terms of availability, OpenAI says both new models will be rolling out throughout the day.

GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for all Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users. Free and Go users can access GPT‑6 Luna in the desktop app. 

You can learn much more about the new models here.

Please welcome GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna to the GPT-6 universe.

GPT-6 Sol and Luna build on the advances behind GPT-6 Astra, bringing much of its strengths into faster and more affordable models to support work at scale.

We’ve also made caching and inference more efficient, and… pic.twitter.com/5LiVE4rbFt

— OpenAI (@OpenAI) September 22, 2026

title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it
snippet: The report suggests that greater exposure will not resolve the unease around the technology, nor reduce public support for AI regulation.
fullText:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations. 

But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently. 

Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI, quick developments around AI safety, the implications of AI going rogue, and accusations of anticompetitive behavior, these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.

Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor are Australia and Malaysia.

The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% of Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.

Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them. 

There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI, with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings, life-ending cases of AI psychosis, and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.

The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. In China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.

Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel, and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.

Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%), and Kenya (87%).

It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. president Donald Trump and Chinese premier Xi Jinping meet on Thursday.

Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”

“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch. 

While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education, or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.

At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

Meta has spent the last two weeks telling anyone who’ll listen how secure its new Muse personal AI agent is. The company boasted about its dedicated Secure VM, a monitoring system called Sentinel, and bug bounty rewards of up to $300,000. Mark Zuckerberg himself even publicly stated the agent is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.”

Then Patrick Wardle, macOS security researcher and friend of Security Bite, found a 0-day vulnerability in the Muse app on Mac that made the last 24 hours particularly not-a-musing (what Wardle comically named the finding).

If you’re struggling to keep track of the AI news cycle too, Muse is Meta’s new personal AI agent, which launched on Mac earlier this month. It’s less of a chatbot and more meant to do things for you across your apps and accounts, like sending emails, filling out forms, handling payments, and making purchases on your behalf. BUT to do all of that, you have to hand it a lot of access (mistake #1).

Wardle found that any app or Terminal command running locally on a Mac can change a number of undocumented Muse settings, no special macOS permissions needed. One of those settings, endo_voyager_dictation_endpoint, controls where your dictated prompts get sent.

An attacker can point that setting away from Meta’s servers, and toward one in their control. So the next time a user dictates a prompt, it goes to the attacker instead. From there, they can grab the token that authenticates your Muse account and use it to control the agent.

Screenshot via Patrick Wardle

Wardle showed this off with a few proof-of-concept attacks, including writing malicious files to the Mac and even taking photos with the camera. He also used a hijacked Muse account to pull the location of a linked iPhone.

To be clear, this doesn’t give a remote attacker instant access to every Mac running Muse. It’s a local attack. They first need a way to run code on your machine. But all it takes is a ClickFix-style attack to trick a Mac user into pasting a command into Terminal. And voilà.

I recorded an entire Security Bite Podcast episode on why ClickFix is the #1 way to get malware on Macs today.

Wardle also pointed out that Apple already offers on-device dictation to developers. If Meta had used it, this bug wouldn’t exist. Instead, Muse sends your voice to its servers to be processed (mistake #2).

The good news is that Meta has reportedly pushed a fix. If you use Muse on Mac, update ASAP.

Hooray, hot-fixed! 😍 Kudos on the quick patch (& full disclosure FTW) 🙏🏽

But there was a 'remote' exploit vector: a simple ClickFix attack could deliver the hijack giving a *remote* attacker complete access then to every victim device running Muse

See: https://t.co/QBszVNCdbn https://t.co/L1dsPkmOgZ

— Patrick Wardle (@patrickwardle) September 22, 2026

snippet: Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. fullText:
Meta announced a slate of new wearables during its annual Meta Connect showcase on Wednesday. The star of the event was the new Meta VR Glasses, which pack virtual reality tech into a lightweight smart glasses-style frame with a tethered puck. Meta also announced new pairs of screen-free smart glasses, along with some new AI features and style and frame options.

You can catch up on all the highlights from this year’s Meta Connect below.

Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge

Meta’s latest wearable offers full virtual reality in a smart glasses-style form factor. Unlike a typical VR headset, the VR Glasses don’t have any straps, and Meta says they’re “five times lighter than Meta Quest 3” at just 100g. Similar to Google’s Project Aura, the glasses are tethered to a pocket-sized puck with the compute hardware, battery, and storage, including a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite, 128GB of storage, and 12GB of RAM. The 5K micro OLED “Infinite Display” has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye, with a refresh rate of up to 120Hz.

The Meta VR Glasses are launching in spring 2027 for $1,299, pricier than the Meta Ray-Ban Display but less expensive than the Apple Vision Pro, while offering similar features. Users can connect the glasses to a Mac or Windows laptop for use as a virtual external display, with an option for a virtual surface keyboard and touchpad.

The VR Glasses also have access to the full Meta Quest catalog of apps and games and support for Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meta says the glasses are “the first IMAX Enhanced certified VR device ever,” and users will be able to watch “immersive live sports” with them as well as 3D movies. They even have a “hologram” feature that creates a “photorealistic digital version of your face” for using in calls while wearing the glasses, reminiscent of the “personas” on the Apple Vision Pro.

Meta is launching camera-free smart glasses

Image: Meta

The highlight of the Ray-Ban Meta Audio is the feature they don’t have: built-in cameras. You can use them for things like listening to music, taking calls, or chatting with an AI assistant, but they can’t take pictures or record video — features that have sparked privacy and harassment concerns around Meta’s other glasses.

Meta says the new audio-only glasses are also its “lightest, slimmest AI glasses yet,” weighing just 43g. They offer up to 12 hours of battery life per charge, or 48 hours with the charging case. The Ray-Ban Meta Audio will launch on October 13th starting at $349 with 23 different color and lens combinations.

Refreshed Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 arrive with battery and design upgrades

Image: Meta

Meta launched an updated version of its main Ray-Ban Meta glasses, starting at $449. The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 offer up to nine hours of battery life, one hour more than the Gen 2. They also have “a new customizable action button for instant access to Meta AI” and a new six-mic array that Meta says “cuts more than 90% of background noise.”

The Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3 has a slimmer design than the Gen 2 as well, with 27 color and lens combinations, including new Zena and Aviator frame styles. Notably, one thing that hasn’t changed is the built-in LED light that indicates when the glasses are recording, which Meta rolled out a privacy fix for last month.

Budget glasses launch along with new glasses styles

Image: Meta

Alongside its pricier Ray-Ban glasses, Meta also announced some updates to its in-house line of glasses. It’s launching a new lower-cost version of the Meta Adventurer, which will start at $249 for a basic design with black frames and gray lenses, launching October 23rd.

Meta is also introducing a new “Mix & Match” program for customizing its glasses with different frames, lenses, and case colors. Plus, its EssilorLuxottica collection is getting two new styles, Capri and Nova, and the Kylie Jenner Starfire frames are getting a new ivory colorway. Meta’s also launching a new collaboration collection with Lisa of Blackpink.

Meta Glasses are expanding to more countries starting today, too, including Singapore, South Korea, Mexico, and the United Arab Emirates, with availability in Brazil “coming soon.”

Meta Ray-Ban Display is coming to more regions with some new features

Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge

A year after they originally launched, the Meta Ray-Ban Display are coming to more regions. The glasses are on sale in the UK and Canada starting today, and they’ll be available in France, Italy, and Germany starting on October 13th. Meta’s also introducing online ordering for customers in those regions and the US.

Meta’s launching a new Explore app for Display glasses where users will be able to “browse and use a growing selection of experiences built for your glasses.” The Meta Ray-Ban Display is also getting photo editing, an improved calendar, and mirrored phone notifications. Plus, Meta says the “hologram” feature launching on its VR Glasses is rolling out on the Meta Ray-Ban Display “in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

Screenshot: The Verge

After launching its new Muse assistant earlier this month, Meta says it’s “working on” bringing the AI to its smart glasses. When it arrives on the glasses, Muse will be able to do things like guide your workouts, log meals, book appointments, and “help buy products you see.”

Meta also announced some new features for Muse, including video calls with a customizable live avatar of the AI. Plus, Muse agents are getting their own email addresses for completing tasks and communicating with users.

Meta is making an AI ‘charm’

Mark Zuckerberg teased one last device, Muse Charm, a small AI gadget that houses the Muse agent and looks a little bit like a supersized Tamagotchi. More details will be shared “soon,” he said, but the product is supposed to ship in time for the holiday season.
