title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone Duo: Comparing Apple’s New Pro Phone Against Its First Foldable
snippet: Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro includes a heck of a camera that sets it apart, but the iPhone Duo’s ability to unfold from small phone to tablet could offer new ways to use an iPhone.
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro is now on sale, but the foldable iPhone Duo is still awaiting its big debut on Oct. 23. While both phones are premium showstoppers, they’re also very different. 

The 18 Pro features the company’s best camera yet on an iPhone, including a variable aperture for the first time. That feature helps you control light exposure, which can improve low-light photography, and you can use the new Pro Controls for additional features, like adjusting shutter speed. And while the outside is similar to the iPhone 17 Pro, the inside has been redesigned to accommodate a larger vapor chamber that helps keep the phone cool during intensive use.

	

			

But it’s the iPhone Duo that really captured people’s attention. It’s Apple’s first foldable phone, with a passport-style design that’s made to fit in your hand when closed. Then you can unfold it like a book to reveal a wide screen that’s almost the size of an iPad Mini (an open iPhone Duo has a 7.6-inch screen while an iPad Mini measures 8.3 inches). Yet, it only has two rear cameras rather than the three that the 18 Pro has, so it won’t have a telephoto lens for zooming into a subject as far as the Pro and Pro Max can. It also doesn’t have the aforementioned variable aperture. 

On top of that, the iPhone Duo is extremely expensive: It starts at $1,999 for the 256GB version. The iPhone 18 Pro isn’t cheap either, but it is less of a stretch, with a starting price of $1,199 for the 256GB version. 

Here are the top highlights for each phone, and you can use our specs chart to compare them further.

The Duo’s inner selfie camera is geared toward FaceTime videos.Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Design and display

The primary difference between the two phones lies in their designs. The iPhone 18 Pro has the usual slab iPhone design that we’ve come to know over the years. It even has the same dimensions as its predecessor, measuring 5.9 by 2.3 by 0.3 inches. This means you can use the same phone cases whether they were designed for the iPhone 17 Pro or the 18 Pro. The 18 Pro has an aluminum unibody design with a triple camera array on the back. On the front is a 6.3-inch OLED display with a 120Hz refresh rate. The display also includes a slimmer Dynamic Island cutout for the front-facing camera and Face ID, which can now display three Live Activities at once.

The iPhone Duo, on the other hand, is quite the departure from Apple as the company’s first foldable. Closed, it has rounded corners on the upper and lower right along with flat titanium sides. Due to its passport size, it has a rather squat 5.4-inch cover display on the front. When it’s closed, it measures 4.6 by 3.3 by 0.4 inches. 

The iPhone Duo when closed.Abrar Al-Heeti/CNET

Open the Duo up, and you will see a 7.6-inch OLED display. While the cover screen has the usual glossy glass display of other iPhones, the main internal display of the iPhone Duo has a matte nano-textured finish designed to reduce reflections and minimize the appearance of the crease. Also, when the Duo is open, it’s just 0.2 inches thick, which is even thinner than last year’s iPhone Air (0.22 inches). Both displays support a 120Hz refresh rate, and the phone can use StandBy mode widgets when folded into a tent-like position. The iPhone Duo doesn’t have Face ID and instead uses a side fingerprint sensor for Touch ID unlocking.

Both phones are IP68-rated for dust and water resistance. That’s particularly notable for the Duo, as it’s one of the few book-style foldable phones to carry that rating. (Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold and 11 Pro Fold are also rated IP68.)

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max on display at Apple’s store on Fifth Avenue in New York for the phones’ launch.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Cameras

The iPhone 18 Pro has the best camera features that Apple has to offer. It has a triple rear camera array: a 48-megapixel wide, ultrawide and telephoto. Its new variable aperture, lets you control how much light hits the sensor, allowing for improved low-light photography, greater depth-of-field for close-up shots and overall a lot more flexibility for creative photography. 

While the iPhone Duo has a compact foldable design as its spotlight feature, its camera system harkens more to what’s included on the iPhone 17. Despite being substantially more expensive than the iPhone 18 Pro, the Duo has a 48-megapixel wide camera and a 48-megapixel ultrawide camera. It does not have a telephoto camera, but its camera system does allow for a 2x optical quality zoom along with a digital zoom to 10x. It also does not have the variable aperture that’s included on the 18 Pro.

Both phones have selfie cameras; the 18 Pro has a 18-megapixel front-facing camera, while the Duo has a 12-megapixel Center Stage selfie camera on the cover display as well as a hidden under-display FaceTime camera on the main display. The benefit of the Duo, however, is that you can actually use the 48-megapixel rear camera as your “selfie” camera when the phone is open as the cover display becomes a viewfinder. 

Apple demonstrated how Netflix will be optimized for the Duo’s displays — from the cover screen to the main display to this half-open configuration with controls on the bottom half. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Performance and battery

Both phones ship with Apple’s latest A20 Pro chip, which is the company’s first to be made with a 2-nanometer process. The processor is therefore denser and should result in a 20% faster CPU and a 40% faster GPU than last year’s A19 Pro. It should also help keep the phone cool even during intensive use. 

As for battery life, Apple doesn’t give the specific capacity for both phones, but it does say that the 18 Pro should last up to 24 hours, while the iPhone Duo will last up to 44 hours while watching videos when closed, and up to 31 hours when open.

The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max is able to show three Live Activities at once.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

In our preliminary test with the 18 Pro, we found that it lasted almost a full day before needing to be charged. It’s also one of the fastest-charging phones CNET has tested, charging from 0% to 82% in just 30 minutes. According to Apple, the iPhone Duo will charge to 50% in about 15 minutes with a 60-watt charger, or to 50% in 30 minutes with a 35-watt wireless MagSafe charger. We’ll have to perform further tests to be sure.

title: Apple releases first iOS 27.2 public beta with new iPhone Health app
snippet: Six days ago, Apple released iOS 27.2 developer beta 1, skipping over iOS 27.1 beta. Following yesterday’s developer beta 2 release, Apple has now issued the first iOS 27.2 public beta version, with the new iPhone Health app included. Apple has also turned on the ability to schedule and purchase labs through Quest Diagnostics from the new Health app in iOS 27.2 beta. more…
fullText:
Six days ago, Apple released iOS 27.2 developer beta 1, skipping over iOS 27.1 beta. Following yesterday’s developer beta 2 release, Apple has now issued the first iOS 27.2 public beta version, with the new iPhone Health app included. Apple has also turned on the ability to schedule and purchase labs through Quest Diagnostics from the new Health app in iOS 27.2 beta.

iOS 27.2 beta includes all-new Health app and more

iOS 27.2 is the next release that will follow the official launch of iOS 27 from September 14. iOS 27.1 is just for iPhone Duo.

Apple has already detailed how the iOS 27.1 SDK will let developers take full advantage of the iPhone Duo display. You can see how apps will appear on iPhone Duo based on which iOS version they target here.

Apple released Xcode 27.1 beta on Friday, adding the iPhone Duo simulator and app development support for the new foldable iPhone.

The first iOS 27.2 developer beta included these changes:

Apple’s redesigned Health app first announced during the iPhone 18 Pro event is now live in this beta.

Dual capture mode comes to Group FaceTime.

Siri AI language support now includes French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish.

Apple TV app profiles come to iPhone.

Up Next is now New Episodes in Apple Podcasts. Continue Playing section is now directly below New Episodes. Podcasts also have color-matched backgrounds on episode lists.

Apple Music uses less of the icon’s color for labels in the app now.

iOS 27.2 is set to be released officially in October. For now, there’s both a developer beta and public beta path for iPhone users looking to test the new Apple Health app early.

title: Muse is coming to Meta smart glasses
snippet: Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it's "working on" bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they're looking at. Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta's glasses. They're also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is "FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss." It will be available lat … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Stevie Bonifield

 

is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Just a couple of weeks after launching Muse, Meta announced that it’s “working on” bringing the agent to its smart glasses, including the new glasses it unveiled at Meta Connect. Users will be able to activate Muse from their glasses by saying its name and ask it to handle tasks like guiding a workout, logging meals, or helping them shop for products they’re looking at.

Muse is just one of several major updates coming to Meta’s glasses. They’re also getting some new accessibility features, like a Hearing Enhancement feature Meta says is “FDA-cleared software for adults with perceived mild to moderate hearing loss.” It will be available later this year with a Meta One subscription or as a $149 add-on for compatible glasses. Meta AI will also be able to give “more context-rich answers” when users ask the glasses what they’re looking at, potentially making Meta’s glasses more effective for helping blind and low-vision users interpret their surroundings. A new audio customization feature will also allow users to shift their smart glasses’ volume between their left and right ears, including sending all audio to one side.

Meta’s introducing some new audio and photo features as well, including Dolby Atmos Capture, which will allow users to record videos with 360-degree spatial audio. A new Dynamic Photo feature automatically captures multiple frames when you take a photo with Meta’s glasses, then uses Meta AI to suggest the best frame from each batch.

The Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are getting the new “Hologram” feature Meta announced for its new VR Glasses, which it says is “a photorealistic digital version of your face for calls from Meta Ray-Ban Display” that “infers” your expression using your voice. The feature’s “rolling out in Early Access on WhatsApp to Meta Ray-Ban Display users in the US later this fall.”

A couple new heads-up navigation features are coming to the Meta Ray-Ban Display as well. Starting later this month, users in the US and Canada will have an option to use their voice to ask for real-time cycling or public transit directions. The Meta Ray-Ban Display will also start using “the world in front of you rather than street signs in turn-by-turn walking directions,” like referencing a house, car, or landmark the glasses detect. A few other new features are on the way for the Display glasses, including an option for editing photos directly on the glasses’ display, a new “Explore” app for finding new apps, an improved calendar, and mirroring for phone notifications.

title: John Ternus talks CEO offer, AI potential, more in new interview
snippet: In a lengthy new interview with Clique TV, Apple CEO John Ternus answered a range of questions covering what excites him about the future, how technology is used in his family, the offer to become CEO, his views on Vision Pro, and more. more…
fullText:
In a lengthy new interview with Clique TV, Apple CEO John Ternus answered a range of questions covering what excites him about the future, how technology is used in his family, the offer to become CEO, his views on Vision Pro, and more.

New John Ternus interview covers wide range of topics as Apple CEO role begins

Clique TV’s Mouloud Achour and Apple’s new CEO John Ternus sat down for an interview earlier this month, which was just published over the weekend.

Ternus discusses a wide range of topics in the interview, including giving a great defense of Apple Vision Pro. As one of his first major interviews as CEO, he is of course asked about that transition.

On being asked to become Apple’s new CEO

Well, I think when when Tim asked me if it was something I would consider, I would say the good news is I was sitting down [laughter] because I never in a million years would have imagined that happening. To me it’s always just been: be here, focus on the work, build great things, love every minute of it. To be given this opportunity, to be asked about it was pretty mind-blowing. It’s beyond words.

Ternus is also asked about the important lessons he learned from his predecessors, Steve Jobs and Tim Cook. He’s asked for specific quotes from Apple’s former leaders that drive him, but Ternus offers something a little different. He says:

What’s kind of the most important lesson I’ve learned from both of them is “focus on the future.” Right? That’s what we do. You know, yesterday was an amazing day. It was so exciting. We launched a product. Today it’s onto the future, onto the next thing.

On the future he’s envisioning at Apple, which includes AI

I think what’s what’s really interesting about this moment is with AI…generative AI, it is a really powerful technology that means this is the most exciting time in my career to be building products because there’s so many new things we can do, things that previously were just science fiction. And so we’re really excited about, like I said before, taking that technology and leveraging it in different ways to build new experiences, new products, new capabilities, and it’s going to be fun.

On the role of technology for children

Ternus also talks about the role of technology, and the iPhone specifically, for children. He touts iOS 27‘s new parental controls that just launched. But when Achour mentions how some tech leaders don’t let their kids use phones or computers, Ternus says: 

Well, I can’t quite relate to that because my kids use them. But it’s something that as a family, we talked about a lot, right? And we managed a lot, and we said, “Here is the time when you can be using these things and these are the things you can use them for, and here are the times when you shouldn’t be on your device.”

The full interview is well worth giving a watch. Additional topics covered include the newly unveiled iPhone Duo and iPhone 18 Pro, whether iPhone users should upgrade models each year, Apple’s involvement in health, and more.

title: Microsoft launches 12-inch Surface Pro with Snapdragon X2 Plus & 5G, 13-inch Surface Laptop too
snippet: Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149. more…
fullText:
Microsoft is rolling out refreshes to its smaller Surface Laptop and Surface Pro machines powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 Plus starting at a price of $1,149.

The Surface Laptop and Surface Pro both picked up their Snapdragon X2 upgrades back in June, but that left the smaller models waiting on refreshes. As a part of Snapdragon Summit, Microsoft is confirming that those will arrive on October 13.

Surface Pro 12-inch is getting a Snapdragon X2 Plus chip, a 25% brighter display, and a battery that’s “30% more efficient.” There’s an optional 5G model coming too, which Microsoft says was “one of the most requested additions.” All models now include either 16GB or 24GB of RAM, removing the 8GB option on last year’s model, with either 256GB or 512GB of storage. 

It’s mostly the same tablet otherwise, just now with a starting price of $1,149. That’s $300 more than the base model sold for, and that’s after a major price hike across the whole lineup back in April. Even directly comparing the 16/256GB model, it’s still a $100 price hike. 

	

The formula is similar on Surface Laptop 13-inch, with this latest generation getting Snapdragon X2 Plus, ditching its 8GB model, and starting at $1,199 – $50 up from the last generation. Again, there are upgrades including a brigher display, but it’s nearly identical to last year’s model outside of the chipset bump.

Microsoft is also launching a new Surface Mouse which has haptic feedback and a customizable Copilot button. It costs $79.99 and will also be available on October 13. Both come with a new “Microsoft Ink Canvas” app.

title: Microsoft Brings Snapdragon X2 to Smallest Surface Pro and Laptop Lines
snippet: The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop get brought up to speed with Qualcomm’s latest processors. And there’s a new Surface Mouse with haptics.
fullText:
I’m the first born in my family, so I haven’t experienced this feeling directly, but my younger brother tells me it wasn’t all that fun when I would get a gift that he was too little to receive along with his big brother (like the time I got my first bike for my 6th birthday while he was still circling our cul-de-sac on a Big Wheel). On Wednesday, Microsoft granted upgrades to its littlest Surface models, which lets them two-wheel around the neighborhood with the bigger models.

The 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop have each been upgraded to Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 series processors, bringing them in line with the larger 13-inch Surface Pro and 13.8- and 15-inch Surface Laptops that received the Snapdragon X2 jolt a few months ago. 

The second-generation Qualcomm processors offer a tick up in application performance and battery life, a larger leap in graphics performance and a giant jump in local AI capabilities, according to Microsoft. My tests with other laptops based on Snapdragon X2 series processors support Microsoft’s estimates.

Along with the two new Surface models, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Mouse that offers haptic feedback. Let’s have a look at the two Surface updates and new mouse.

12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition)

The new 12-inch Surface Pro is based on a Snapdragon X2 Plus processor and available in business black.Katie Collins/CNET

The second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro trots out the same design as the inaugural model, but inside it has moved to a six-core Snapdragon X Plus X2P-42-100. You are actually giving up two cores from the previous Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 but getting a more advanced X2-45 integrated GPU and neural processing unit. The NPU is designed for the integer math required for AI tasks, and the Snapdragon X2’s NPU is capable of 80 trillion operations per second. That’s nearly double the 45 TOPS of the NPU of the first-gen Snapdragon X Plus.

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) also ups the memory, giving you the choice of 16GB or 24GB of RAM. That’s an increase from the previous 8GB and 16GB options. Storage remains the same and rather uninspired: 256GB or 512GB.

The display also stays the same: a 12-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a resolution of 2,196×1,464 pixels and 90Hz refresh rate. The only difference is it’s 25% brighter, pushing the max brightness from 400 to 500 nits.

And there’s a new color option, but it might not excite you. In addition to platinum and violet, the new 12-inch Surface Pro comes in black. The bluish-gray ocean color has been discontinued.

The new 12-inch Surface Pro comes preinstalled with Microsoft Ink Canvas, a new AI-powered app for sketching, annotating, generating images and summarizing text directly on the screen with the Slim Pen. 

The 12-inch Surface Pro (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13, starting at $1,150. As with all Surface Pro pricing, the starting price is misleading because Microsoft charges extra for accessories, including the keyboard. Microsoft hasn’t divulged accessory pricing, but the keyboard for the first-gen 12-inch Surface Pro, which is very much needed, adds $150 to the bill. Still, it’s nice that the entry-level model starts at 16GB of RAM, saving you from having to spend extra to move up from the meager 8GB.

13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition)

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) looks no different than the first edition, but it offers newer Qualcomm processors, more RAM and a brighter display.Katie Collins/CNET

The 13-inch Surface Laptop has two big brothers in the 13.8-inch Surface Laptop and 15-inch model. They have each offered Snapdragon X2 series processors since May or June, and now the smallest Surface Laptop gets its Snapdragon X2 upgrade. It offers the same configuration options as the new 12-inch Surface Pro:

Qualcomm Snapdragon X Plus X1P-42-100 CPU

16GB or 24GB RAM

256GB or 512GB SSD

There’s no change to the display other than the same bump in brightness as the second-gen 12-inch Surface Pro got. It’s a 13-inch PixelSense touch LCD with a 3:2 aspect ratio, a pixel resolution of 1,920×1,280 and a 60Hz refresh rate, but it is now rated for 500 nits of brightness. It also comes in the same three colors as the new 12-inch Surface Pro: platinum, violet and black.

Microsoft says you can expect up to 22.5 hours of battery life from the second-gen 13-inch Surface Laptop. That would actually be slightly shorter if our tests bear that out. The previous 13-inch Surface Laptop lasted more than 24 hours in testing.

The 13-inch Surface Laptop (2nd Edition) will be available on Oct. 13 starting at $1,199.

Surface Mouse (2nd Edition)

The new Surface Mouse has haptics to provide physical, tactile feedback.Katie Collins/CNET

If you’re more of a mouser than a touchpad user, Microsoft has a new mouse it’s hoping you’ll pick up with your next Surface purchase. The most interesting part about the second-generation Surface Mouse is the inclusion of haptics that offer tactile feedback across its entire surface. These pulses can confirm clicks, drags, alignment and other actions in apps including PowerPoint, Concepts, Affinity by Canva and Filmora.

The Surface Mouse also adds a customizable action button that sits in front of the scroll wheel. The Bluetooth 6.0 mouse will be available in black and platinum for $80. Like the new Surface computers, the Surface Mouse (2nd Edition) will start shipping on Oct. 13.

title: Meta launches audio-only glasses and Gen 3 Ray-Ban with slimmer designs
snippet: Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release. more…
fullText:
Meta today introduced its new Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) smart glasses with a slimmer design and longer battery life alongside a new audio-only lineup, and a new $250 entry-level release.

Despite public backlash in recent months, smart glasses continue to explode in popularity and, as it stands, Meta is by far the biggest player in the game. Today’s event further saw the company digging in on its smart glasses success with three new releases.

The self-branded Meta Glasses lineup is adding new styles that start at just $249. A new pair of Meta Adventurer glasses will be available with a black frame and grey lenses and a plug-in case. They’re available starting October 23. 

Next in line is a pair of audio-only glasses, Ray-Ban Meta Audio. Starting at $349 in October, these glasses ditch the camera and, in turn, also deliver a much slimmer form factor. They weigh 43g and run for 12 hours on a single charge (48 hours in the case). Meta says the new hardware features “professional-adjustable temple tips, adjustable or swappable nose pads, and overextension hinges.” 

	

Styles include “Clubmaster” and “Burbank” in a variety of frame and lens styles.

Beyond that, Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) is available today starting at $449. Meta says to expect longer battery life – 9 hours, an hour longer than Gen 2 – and the same camera capabilities, including 3K video recording. The hardware is slimmer and adds professional-adjustable temple tips. 

Meta is also launching this latest generation in way more styles, with 27 combinations across “Aviator,” “Wayfarer,” and cateye “Zena” frame styles.

You can order Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3) now through Meta’s store.

Finally, Meta is also upgrading its Display glasses with hands-free navigation, “Hologram” personas for video calls, new apps, notification mirroring from your phone, and Threads integration. Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses are also expanding to the UK, Canada, France, Italy, and Germany, and you can finally order them online in the US, still priced at $799.

title: From Audio Glasses to Earbuds With Cameras, Headphones Are Getting a Major AI Rebrand
snippet: In the age of agentic AI, headphones are no longer the straightforward audio devices they once were.
fullText:
You’ve likely noticed AI has increasingly been sneaking into more of your new devices over the past few years, whether you asked for it or not. The next frontier? It’s time to ready yourself for an influx of AI-powered headphones.

On Wednesday at its Snapdragon Summit in Hawaii, Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 chip, which will bring new features to audio wearables, or “hearables,” as they’re sometimes referred to in the tech industry. These might look and feel like the audio products you’ve been strapping to your head for many years, but they’ll have a whole different set of features and capabilities.

Plaud One brings AI note-taking to headphones.Plaud/CNET

Some might use AI to provide you with a better sound experience, improving music quality and making your headphones able to more intelligently adapt to your world – identifying an approaching siren and lowering the volume of your music so you know not to step onto the road, for example. Others might use AI to enable real-time translation as a conduit for interacting with agents or for note-taking, like the recently revealed Plaud One. Hidden use case C could enable so-called multimodal interactions – for example, combining audio with vision and AI in audio-forward glasses or headphones with cameras.

Qualcomm envisages the Sound Elite Gen 2 chip being used in a range of different audio devices. These include the usual suspects – earbuds, headphones, open-ear and hybrid audio devices. But it also says they can be used in audio glasses and “future multimodal wearables” – a vague term that can be broadly interpreted as new types of product that haven’t been invented yet.

Qualcomm’s chips are designed both with specific devices in mind and for companies to run with and build something new. Just take last year’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5: It was designed for top Android phones, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 series, but it was also used by Honor to build its Robot Phone – a novel handset with a built-in robotic gimbal.

While there’s some level of predictability to the types of devices the Sound Elite Gen 2 will feature in, the platform is also open-ended enough for companies to use it in ways even Qualcomm hasn’t foreseen. Ziad Asghar, a senior vice president at the company, said that he’s surprised “all the time” at what the chipmaker’s partners dream up.

“The innovation [in] form factor right now is still morphing, it’s still changing,” he said. “We don’t know what end product [the chip] might even go into.”

What’s new in the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 Chip?

The footprint of this latest Sound Elite chip is 30% smaller than that of its predecessor, as well as having double the AI capability and offering up to 40% lower power consumption. This combination of being smaller, more powerful and more power efficient is the chip upgrade trifecta, but what difference will that actually make?

Qualcomm thinks it will move you closer to your personal AI future. This is the idea that thanks to your always-sensing, always-on galaxy of devices – which could include your watch, phone, glasses, earbuds, car and home tech – the combination of constant context capture and AI agents will enable better understanding of your wants and needs.

The new chip will enable next-generation AI wearables.

Hearables play an important role in bringing the vision for personal AI to life because they sit close to your ears and mouth, allowing for both input and output of audio.

“As AI becomes a core capability, users will increasingly expect more natural ways to interact with it,” said Asghar, speaking at the Snapdragon Summit. “Those interactions won’t always happen through a screen. They will happen through natural conversations, where users can simply speak to an AI assistant and receive help in real time.”

Another technical aspect of making this happen is the Sound Elite Gen 2 chip’s direct-to-cloud connectivity, enabled by micro-power Wi-Fi 6E. This technology was designed to give Wi-Fi connectivity with the power of Bluetooth inside tiny products. For the generation included in this chip, Qualcomm has reduced the power requirements even further and increased the speed to provide always-on availability.

Additionally, the chip will include Qualcomm aptX Lossless – an audio quality boost to appease the audiophiles among us – and Qualcomm XPAN, which extends connectivity beyond the range you’d typically expect from Bluetooth. Qualcomm is also deploying AI to improve active noise cancellation, speech capture and voice clarity by providing more advanced support for multiple mics.

Keep your ear to the ground for devices making use of this chip for more personalized and intelligent audio experiences – and remember, they might not look exactly how you expect them to.

Editors’ note: Katie Collins’ travel costs were covered by Qualcomm. The judgments and opinions of CNET are our own.

title: Meta ditches the camera on its newest smart glasses
snippet: The Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses have no cameras. | Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone's sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It's a marked difference here, a tech bubble where "pervert glasses" are not a concern. Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech - a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants - is gaining steam. So it's incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others. To hear Meta tell it, that's a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Walking around Meta Connect 2026, everyone’s sporting smart glasses in all sorts of shapes, colors, and sizes. It’s a marked difference here, a tech bubble where “pervert glasses” are not a concern.

Outside Connect, the public backlash against wearable surveillance tech — a catchall term that encompasses not just smart glasses, but also smartwatches and AI pendants — is gaining steam. So it’s incredibly curious timing that this year, the company is launching Ray-Ban Meta Audio Glasses: smart glasses infused with Meta AI, but with no camera for recording others.

To hear Meta tell it, that’s a coincidence. Audio-only glasses have been years in the making.

“Three years ago, it wasn’t clear if AI glasses were going to be a thing. Back then, every other company was backing out of the space,” says Alex Himel, Meta’s vice president of wearables. “Then two years ago, we saw that audio was the top use case, the biggest potential for AI, and that it should work well in a pair of audio glasses.”

Himel has a point. Open-ear audio is the least controversial part of the Ray-Bans — and the thing everyone can agree is convenient. Plus, the camera-less glasses are lighter. Himel says that by removing the cameras, Meta could “rearchitect” the glasses. “That allowed us to take a lot of electronics out of the front frame and have a lot more design flexibility.”

The audio-only models start at 43 grams — heavier than normal wire-frame glasses, but noticeably lighter than the roughly 50g Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 and the 69g Meta Ray-Ban Display. The arms are thinner. They come in two styles: the Mad Men-esque Clubmaster and the more Wayfarer-reminiscent Burbank. The hinges extend for wider faces; the temple arms and nose pads are adjustable. There are 23 color and lens combinations, and they can support the same wider prescription range as the Ray-Ban Meta Optics lineup. Even more so than the standard Meta Ray-Bans, these look and wear like normal glasses. And with a $349 starting price, they’re cheaper too.

Free of a power-hungry camera, the battery lasts an estimated 12 hours on a single charge. The most technical things you can do with them are interact with Meta AI, take phone calls, and listen to podcasts or music. And that’s it.

“They don’t record,” Himel says. “The only thing they do, which is the same thing as an Alexa device in your house or some other devices, they’re just listening for a specific wake word. They’re not sending anything … If they hear [the wake word], then they start listening to what you’re saying. When you’re done talking, then it’s processing, and that’s visible to the AI. It gets processed, and that’s kind of it.”

Slipping them on, they’re comfortable and, I think, quite fetching on me. Regardless of how one might feel about Meta, it’s fair to guess most people would feel less like a creeper wearing these.

Meta Glasses and Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3

I feel differently slipping on the new Ray-Ban Meta Gen 3. Partly because the camera is back in play, partly because the pair Meta gives me is the new aviator style with transition lenses. I’m told I can pull it off, but I keep asking my colleague Jay Peters if I’m giving ’80s serial killer vibes. The other new style is called Zena — not the warrior princess — and it’s a bolder, geometric cat-eye frame.

The third-generation glasses feature fairly minor refinements. There’s a sixth microphone, compared to the second generation’s five, for clearer phone calls. Battery life has gotten a slight boost to nine hours, an hour longer than the second gen. The temple arms, like the audio-only glasses, are adjustable for a better fit. All sound will now be captured in Dolby Atmos for spatial audio. Sure! That’s neat if I’m in my quiet hotel room, but it’s harder to appreciate when reviewing footage amid the hustle and bustle of Meta Connect. The new model comes in 27 color and lens combinations, plus three seasonal options.

Along with the hardware changes, the Gen 3 glasses are also getting a price bump. They start at $449, up from $379 for the second-gen models last year.

Meta Glasses — the off-brand, more affordable entry-level glasses launched a few months ago — also have more options. There are two new styles, Capri and Nova. Capri is some kind of cat-eye shape, while Nova… honestly, the styles are all starting to blur together. They’re round and remind me of several other Ray-Ban Meta glasses, but slightly different. There’s a new ivory-colored Kylie Jenner pair that costs $399.

But maybe Kylie Jenner isn’t the celebrity collab you’ve been dreaming about. That’s fine. Because Blackpink’s Lisa — a K-pop icon and The White Lotus actress — also has Meta Glasses. They have pink lenses and come with a blind-box-type charm styled after Lisa’s pets. These also start at $399. (Non-celebrity versions of the Meta Glasses start at $249.)

Why the celebrity collabs? Options for more people, including women.

“With the Meta Glasses Starfire with Kylie, we saw a younger, more female audience start to buy the glasses,” says Himel. “Wayfarer is the most popular glasses type in the world, but it tends to be more male — though definitely not exclusively male. The second brand we did was Oakley … but Oakley [also] tends to be a more masculine brand. So I think with Kylie and Lisa, and with more styles, we’re seeing them appeal to more women.”

There are actually more limited-edition versions, styles, colors, and prescription permutations available across the entire existing Ray-Ban Meta lineup at a whole range of price points. I suspect I’d need to make a spreadsheet to list them all. While scuttling about Meta’s campus this week, I’m brought to an entire area where they’re all displayed. It looks like a high-end store for, regular, schmegular glasses. That, I suspect, is the whole point.

AI in your frames

All around the campus, there are life-size cutouts of Meta’s cuddly Muse mascot. That’s because Muse, Meta’s recently released personal AI agent, is coming to the seemingly 4,000 iterations of Meta smart glasses that now exist.

“Muse is gonna be everywhere,” confirms Himel. “Muse is gonna be on every device that we make.”

The pitch for Muse in your glasses is that your AI assistant will better remember your context and do things on your behalf. During a demo, I ask a Muse agent to help me buy snacks that will give me the best protein bang for my calorie buck. It can do it, but fails at adding another snack to my cart. Obviously, this is an early-stage demo, and there are always kinks. I can see the shape of how this could be helpful. I can also see how it’d be a treasure trove of data for Meta.

Less contentious is a demo of a new FDA-cleared hearing assistance feature. I’m asked to wear earplugs to mimic mild hearing loss. Things sound a bit muddled. With the feature turned on, higher voices gain a tinny quality as the AI works to boost conversational tones in a semi-loud environment. After about five minutes, I’ve forgotten I have earplugs in. Adding this capability will cost an extra $149, but I’m told it’s FSA/HSA eligible and designed to be a one-time fee versus an ongoing subscription.

Lastly, there are two minor privacy updates — though neither truly addresses the fears people have been debating this past summer. The first is bringing the same “private processing” pipeline used on WhatsApp to wearables. It’s a server-based system in which a user’s data is inaccessible to Meta or any other third parties when end-to-end encryption isn’t possible or on-device processing isn’t powerful enough.

“It’s so that you know that your data is just yours and you’re the only one who has access to it. Other companies have taken an approach to everything on-device. We do a lot on-device. But the problem with just doing things on-device is that the device is only so powerful and capable. And so if you want to run more capable models and get better functionality, we want to offer the same privacy protections, but with more capabilities. So that’s what private processing is,” says Himel.

Meta will also roll out an update where users can opt out of their visual data being used for AI training. (Audio-only queries are still used for training.)

That’s progress but doesn’t really address people’s primary concerns about the glasses being used to covertly record people in public. Himel also acknowledges that the private processing feature is mostly about protecting the data of the person wearing the glasses.

More is more

Meta’s goal at Connect this year is to bombard everyone with options. By the end of the year, Meta expects to have over 100 versions of its glasses. The more versions of its glasses, the more people they’ll reach. The more AI updates that trickle to each of these iterations, the faster Meta can stake its claim on the next era of mobile computing.

So goes the theory. But providing hardware options isn’t Meta’s problem. Inside the safe bubble of Meta’s campus, everyone wears these glasses. The issue is outside Menlo Park, where a vocal contingent isn’t asking for more. They’re asking for less.

title: Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI GPT-6 Sol & Luna both launch today with lower costs
snippet: Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other. more…
fullText:
Anthropic and OpenAI are both launching new model updates today, with Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol & Luna both being announced within roughly an hour of each other.

Claude Opus 5.5 was up to bat first today, so we’ll start there. 

Anthropic explains that its latest model update performs at the level of Claude Fable 5.1 on “most work” while cutting costs to run by around 40% compared to Opus 5 – which was already around half the price of Fable 5. 

Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

Despite the lower compute costs, Anthropic says that Opus 5.5 is more powerful, beating out Fable 5.1 in every metric and beating OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra in virtually every category measured as well including metrics such as agentic coding, knowledge work, and more. 

	

Claude Opus 5.5 is available now on “all platforms,” Anthropic says.

And that’s not all. OpenAI, roughly an hour after Claude’s announcement, launched its GPT-6 Sol & Luna models, also focused on costs.

Like Opus 5.5, OpenAI says that GPT-6 Sol and Luna are both much more affordable to run compared to their GPT-5.6 counterparts. Specifically, they’re both about 50% less expensive when measuring input and output per 1 million tokens in API use. 

Both models are marginally more powerful than their predecessors, but well behind that of Astra, which remains the overall most powerful model OpenAI offers. Luna prioritizes cost over capability, while Sol strikes a balance between the two by offering more horsepower than Luna but at a more affordable cost compared to Astra.

We trained GPT‑6 Sol and Luna with similar methods as GPT‑6 Astra, bringing the advances behind Astra’s state-of-the-art performance in professional work, factuality, coding, computer use, and alignment to faster, more affordable models.

The GPT‑6 models lead across the cost–intelligence curve, combining exceptional capabilities at every tier with infrastructure that delivers them efficiently at scale. Improvements in caching and inference let us serve these models at lower cost, and we’re passing those savings directly on to users and customers by reducing API prices for Sol and Luna by 50% compared with their GPT‑5.6 promotional pricing.

OpenAI says Sol and Luna are available in ChatGPT Work and Codex starting today for Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu users, while Luna is available in the desktop app for Free and Go users. Neither model is available in Chat just yet.

As part of Made on YouTube 2026, a handful of updates to YouTube Music that are coming later this year were previewed.

After moving search to the bottom bar earlier this year, YouTube Music is placing the Gemini spark icon in the top-right corner of the mobile app to let you access Ask Music. This more consistent entry point — compared to the Home feed card — slides up a sheet with the chat experience.

This “completely eyes-optional and hands-free” experience leverages audio gen AI capabilities. Testing will start later this year for subscribers worldwide.

title: Black Workers Allege Systemic Racism at Tesla as Landmark California Trial Begins
snippet: State regulators presented evidence of unaddressed discrimination, wage disparities and hostile conditions on the EV maker’s Fremont assembly line.
fullText:
Tesla is facing a major civil rights lawsuit due to years of alleged rampant racist behavior against dozens of Black employees at its flagship Fremont assembly factory in California.

During opening statements on Monday, California Civil Rights Department attorney Brett Watson presented evidence of severe workplace harassment at Tesla, as reported by The Guardian. Photos and court documents revealed swastikas carved into factory surfaces, widespread use of the N-word, images of Confederate flags and other white supremacist symbols across the Fremont plant.

Black employees reported receiving harassing messages, such as: “Go back to Africa,” and “You want to hang from a tree?”

The allegations extend beyond harassment, as several Black workers say Elon Musk’s company subjected them to unequal pay and were given inferior job assignments and fewer opportunities for career advancement than other employees. Complaints of unchecked systemic racism at Tesla’s Fremont plant date back to 2012. The current lawsuit was filed 10 years later, in 2022.

This isn’t the first time Tesla has been involved in a legal battle over racial discrimination. Also in 2022, a former Tesla worker at the Fremont plant, Owen Diaz, was awarded over $3 million in damages for similar racial discrimination accusations.

Tesla has denied any wrongdoing, calling the lawsuit “misguided” and suggesting the company is the real victim.

Tesla’s lead attorney, Tyree Jones, countered the state’s claims during opening arguments by repeatedly uttering the racial slur to illustrate his defense. Jones argued that in the context of the factory floor, the N-word was frequently used as a casual greeting among Black workers rather than a derogatory insult.

Because this is a bench trial, no jury will be present throughout the case. Judge Peter Borkon will determine whether Tesla violated California’s civil rights laws. If the state wins, it’s very possible Borkon could force Tesla to overhaul its labor policies and HR practices.

Given that this is one of Tesla’s most prominent factories, the judge’s ruling could have ripple effects throughout Silicon Valley, impacting workplace equity policies, while also serving as a test of the state’s strict antidiscrimination laws. The trial is expected to conclude in late October.

Tesla and the California Civil Rights Department didn’t immediately reply to our request for comment.

title: Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Opus 5.5 model, details here
snippet: Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Opus 5.5. The new version arrives about two months after the previous Opus model upgrade, matching Anthropic’s previous upgrade cadence. more…
fullText:
Anthropic has released its latest AI model with Claude Opus 5.5. The new version arrives about two months after the previous Opus model upgrade, matching Anthropic’s previous upgrade cadence.

Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5

Anthropic currently offers a few AI models under the Claude umbrella. 

The three main models are Haiku (smallest and cheapest), Sonnet (medium size and price), and Opus (largest and most expensive of the three).

There’s also Fable/Mythos, which is even more capable and costly, which represents Anthropic’s highest tier.

Opus 5.5 is here! 🎉  It's honestly such a nice model to work with. 

Feels like Fable, but ~30% faster and ~40% cheaper per task than Opus 5. Go try it out! pic.twitter.com/zwo83sbgez

— Lydia Hallie ✨ (@lydiahallie) September 22, 2026

Today’s release upgrades Claude’s Opus model from version 5 to version 5.5.

“Opus 5.5 is our first model since we called for pacing the frontier,” Anthropic says. “As with previous models, it was tested by external evaluators before release, including METR and Frontier Design. On our most comprehensive alignment test, it achieves the strongest score to date.”

Here’s what Anthropic says about Opus 5.5 performance:

Opus 5.5 is a major step up from Opus 5. It’s the new leading model, and early testers saw large jumps in performance on their most complex work. One tester completed a 680,000-line code migration in less than a day—work that would have taken an engineering team weeks. It’s good at finding and fixing inefficiencies in software: when we asked it to cut load times across every page of a web app, Opus 5.5 succeeded 39 of 40 times, while Opus 5 made smaller improvements that also altered the app’s behavior. A different tester had several Claude models build a game from a single prompt; Opus 5.5 scored higher than any other model on the strength of its graphics and polish.

When it comes to coding specifically, here’s what Anthropic says:

Opus 5.5 is particularly good at long and sprawling jobs like codebase-wide migrations and audits. An early tester used it to audit and fix a 200,000-line codebase in under three hours, where Opus 5 took over 20 hours and used 2.5x as many tokens. In an internal test, we asked Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 to translate HAProxy, widely used software that balances web traffic loads across servers, from C into Rust. Both rewrites passed nearly all of HAProxy’s own regression tests, but Opus 5.5 finished in 9.5 hours compared to 12 for Fable 5.1, and cost 51% less.

Opus 5.5 delivers frontier results on agentic coding at a fraction of the cost. At its default effort level on FrontierCode, it beats GPT-6 Astra at roughly 20% of the cost per task. On Terminal Bench 4.0, it matches Astra for about 40% of the cost, while on CursorBench it beats GPT-5.6 Sol by 11 points for about a third of the cost.

Additionally, pricing has been adjusted for Opus 5.5 compared to Opus 5:

Opus 5.5 requires less compute to serve than Opus 5, and its pricing reflects that. Our tests show that at default settings it will cost 40% less than Opus 5 on typical workloads. Input and output tokens are $4 and $20 per million, 20% less than Opus 5. Cache reads (which make up the majority of agentic and coding work costs) are $0.20 per million tokens, 60% less than Opus 5. Opus 5.5 also generates output more than 30% faster than Opus 5.

In addition to the price drop, we’re increasing five-hour usage limits on Pro, Max, and Team plans. We’re also providing subscription users a rate limit reset, which you can now save and use whenever you choose.

The new Claude Opus 5.5 model is now available. Looking ahead, Anthropic says both Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Haiku 5.5 models will arrive “in the coming weeks, with many of the same improvements to performance, efficiency, and safety.”

You can learn much more about the new Claude Opus 5.5 model here.

title: New Phishing Attack Promises Claude Max, but Steals Your Google Credentials Instead
snippet: Malwarebytes reports that the scam, which appears as a website offer from Anthropic, is not as easy to detect as most.
fullText:
The offer is for access to about $200 worth of Anthropic’s Claude Max service. But the real price could be giving scammers access to everything in your Google accounts.

A new phishing scam reported by the cybersecurity service Malwarebytes works like this: The scam claims that Anthropic is celebrating attracting 100 million users by giving 10,000 people a free month of Claude Max with x20 limits. The offer, which includes “extended thinking” and “priority access to Opus and Sonnet, no caps,” is actually all cap. It’s a fake offer that leads to a Google login page meant to steal login and password information, which could in turn open up access to Gmail, Google Docs and other non-Google accounts that use your Google information.

The fake giveaway, Malwarebytes said in its report, is different from many other phishing attempts because of how convincing it looks.

“The presentation is careful, down to the real logo and colors, invented five-star reviews, and a long footer whose links lead almost entirely to genuine Anthropic pages,” wrote Stefan Dasic, senior malware research engineer at Malwarebytes. The page also includes a running counter showing how many of those fake 10,000 accounts have been given away.

For those who fall for the scam, clicking on the offer leads to a login page to upgrade a Claude account. An Apple login option is disabled, leaving only the option to “Sign in with Google.” The login page employs a browser-in-a-browser trick that Dasic said is convincing enough to fool those who don’t look carefully. “The page draws a browser window inside the existing tab, complete with a padlock and a correctly spelled Google sign-in address. It can even be dragged around the page.”

In a message to CNET, Dasic said that the login prompt might convince those who don’t take the time to examine the login page. “The overlap matters because Claude has no password of its own: You get in either by continuing with Google or by a login link sent to your email. So if someone’s Claude account is tied to the Google account that was phished, the attacker reaches it either way.”

How to spot fake browser scams like this

Dasic told CNET that it’s too early to tell how widespread the scam has gone or how many people it’s reached. So far, he said, an investigation has traced the site to a UK-registered company, but the server is rented, “which tells us where the server was rented, not who rented it.”

The web page has components that contain developer comments written in Russian; it could, however, be part of a tool built by someone who isn’t necessarily the scammer involved in this campaign.

“Language in code is weak evidence on its own and has been planted before to misdirect,” Dasic added.

Malwarebytes offered a few tips in its post for detecting a fake browser window:

For a popup login screen, try dragging the window outside the browser. A real popup won’t be trapped inside the web page.

Let your password manager determine if it’s providing information to a real site. If it doesn’t populate the text boxes, that’s a good signal that it’s fake.

If you arrived on a site through a link, verify it by trying to find it on the company’s actual website. In this case, you wouldn’t find it on Anthropic’s website.

Don’t fall for single sign-in options. The disabled login for Apple is an indication that the scammer is trying to steer people into its trap.

Slot counters and countdowns aren’t a sign that a website is legitimate or that an offer is real.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Omar Gallaga

He lives in the Texas Hill Country.

title: iOS 27 adds an all-new app to your iPhone’s Home Screen
snippet: Apple released iOS 27 to everyone last week, including a ton of new Siri and Apple Intelligence features. One of the biggest changes here is the addition of an all-new Siri app. This marks the first time that Siri has been pre-installed as a standalone app for iPhone users … more…
fullText:
Apple released iOS 27 to everyone last week, including a ton of new Siri and Apple Intelligence features. One of the biggest changes here is the addition of an all-new Siri app. This marks the first time that Siri has been pre-installed as a standalone app for iPhone users …

The Siri app in iOS 27

After you update to iOS 27, you’ll see the new Siri icon appear on your iPhone’s Home Screen. This app is also coming to the Mac with macOS 27, Vision Pro with visionOS 27, iPad with iPadOS 27, and Apple Watch with watchOS 27.

The Siri app in iOS 27 lets you revisit all your conversations with Siri and easily start new ones. The Siri app syncs with iCloud, so you can continue conversations across all of your Apple devices. It features a chat-style interface with a stream of your previous conversations. You can also upload photos and files to the Siri app for analysis.

The Siri app ties into the new Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities introduced in iOS 27. This includes access to broad world knowledge, personal context of everything on your iPhone, and much more. Siri AI can also recognize what’s on your screen and answer questions about it.

With access to that personal context, Siri AI can reference things like your messages, emails, photos, and more to answer your specific questions. 

Siri app compatibility in iOS 27

The Siri app, however, won’t be coming to all iPhone models. It will be available on devices that support Apple Intelligence, which covers the iPhone 15 Pro and newer:

iPhone 15 Pro

iPhone 15 Pro Max

iPhone 16

iPhone 16e

iPhone 16 Plus

iPhone 16 Pro

iPhone 16 Pro Max

iPhone 17

iPhone 17e

iPhone Air

iPhone 17 Pro

iPhone 17 Pro Max

Wrap up

Apple has recently added several new iPhone apps by default, including Image Playground as part of iOS 18.2 in December 2024. Last year’s iOS 26 update added the new Preview and Games apps for iPhone users.

title: Opera’s free built-in VPN can now turn on automatically when using public Wi-Fi
snippet: Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Opera announced today that its free, built-in VPN for desktop can now automatically activate when users connect to public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Here are the details.

Opt-in feature rolls out today in the US and France

Since 2016, the Opera browser has offered a free, built-in VPN. The company says this builds on its core belief that “making basic online privacy accessible to everyone.”

In recent years, VPNs have gone from being a relatively niche privacy tool to something much more mainstream. Still, according to data from We Are Social’s Digital 2026 Mid-Year Global Update Report, only 23% of internet users aged 16 and older use a VPN for at least some of their online activities.

That is a problem, particularly for users who rely on public Wi-Fi for work or while traveling.

Today, Opera announced that users in the US and France can opt to have its built-in VPN turn on automatically whenever they connect to a public or unsecured Wi-Fi network.

Here’s Opera:

Public Wi-Fi networks are notoriously vulnerable to snooping and data interception. Opera’s browser VPN now removes manual friction by automatically activating when detecting public or unsecured Wi-Fi networks. Users can study, work, manage finances, or browse without having to remember to turn on protection manually. To respect user agency, the feature remains strictly opt-in and can be easily toggled within settings. This functionality is rolling out today to Opera users in the US and France.

Opera notes that its “free VPN operates under strict GDPR laws,” adding that it “has been independently audited by Deloitte.” The company also stresses that the VPN is part of a broader set of built-in privacy tools, alongside Opera’s native Ad Blocker and Tracker Blocker.

title: I Wore Meta’s New $1,299 VR Glasses: A Tiny Quest, or Vision Pro to Go?
snippet: Meta’s not done with VR. Its sleek and expensive glasses-like VR device doesn’t need controllers, plays Quest games and is aiming to be your personal cinema too.
fullText:
I could see the whole room in front of me in surprisingly crisp color video detail, while looking at a grid of apps in front of me. Selecting an app with my eyes and a pinch of my fingers, I launched a 3D Billie Eilish concert video. Then I watched an immersive NBA game that stretched all around me. Was I on the Apple Vision Pro? No, I was wearing a pair of Meta VR Glasses, Meta’s $1,299 reimagining of its VR ecosystem coming next spring that feels like one part Apple, one part Meta Quest and one part AR glasses that haven’t been built yet.

Despite releasing waves of smart glasses over the last few years and ditching games studios, software initiatives and fitness apps, including Supernatural earlier this year, Meta’s not done with VR. But the Meta VR Glasses are a very different proposition than the Quest: in price, in design, in portability and in ambition. They’re not AR glasses, like Meta’s Orion prototype I tried two years ago. But they are a VR headset in glasses form, and share a lot in common with the Orion.

I felt echoes of other products as I slipped Meta’s new visor-like pair of VR glasses over my head. An Apple Vision Pro that’s been put onto folding glasses. No: a Meta Quest Pro shrunken down. Or, the Xreal Aura I tried earlier this year. The Meta VR Glasses – yes, that’s their real name – feel like they’re straddling gadget categories. And they’re pushing a price Meta hasn’t tried for in years.

Meta unveiled the VR Glasses on Wednesday at its Connect developer conference, along with camera-free Meta Ray-Bans and an FDA-cleared hearing enhancement feature and plans to install its Muse AI agent across its lineup of smart glasses.

Meta VR Glasses, when folded, are seriously compact. Scott Stein/CNET

Ultraportable VR

The best point of comparison for the Meta VR Glasses might be the now-discontinued Quest Pro, from their small size to their vivid displays and eye- and hand-tracking controls. But they’re also oddly evolutionary, like many other recent VR/AR products I’ve tried.

The magnesium frame glasses-like visor looks minimal compared to any other VR headset, but I’ve seen this form before. I wore another “VR glasses” device called the URXR One back in June. 

Meta’s VR Glasses wired to the processor puck. They work as a team.Scott Stein/CNET

I felt like I was wearing a smaller, like a sliced-off front end of an Apple Vision Pro, bonded to a pair of glasses’ arms. The curved front visor is studded with cameras and sensors that can sense movement in front of and well below my field of view: I could gently pinch my fingers while resting them on the table, the sort of lazy interactions I can do on the Vision Pro. Volume buttons and another control button are embedded in the arms.

The processor puck is where the one USB-C passthrough port is located, and devices that input through it can stream that device into the VR environment, something I didn’t get to try. The puck comes with 128GB of storage, but also has a MicroSD card slot for expandable storage, which requires higher-speed cards. Still, it’s a first for Meta’s VR headsets.

The color passthrough video quality, which makes virtual experiences look projected into the room like augmented reality, was a big notch up from the Quest 3. It felt close to where Samsung and Apple are with their more expensive headsets.

Meta scanned my eyeglasses to provide prescription lens inserts that matched my vision. The inserts fit into the clear pancake lenses in the visor, which were covered in a soft mesh much like the inside of the Vision Pro headset. The Meta VR glasses fit well on my face, too, and they’re far lighter than wearing a Quest 3. They’re 100 grams, which is heavy for glasses but very, very light for a VR headset. They come in two different sizes, but I’m not sure which one I tried.

The lenses in Meta VR Glasses are small, but the viewing experience is impressive.Scott Stein/CNET

My hands-on time with the Meta VR Glasses

I controlled everything with my hands and eyes, because the Meta VR Glasses don’t come with any controllers at all. They’ll work with Meta Quest controllers, and new controllers will be sold separately, but the whole device is designed to work controller-free. Meta’s promising a series of new optimized games for the headset that will be eye and hand-tracking controlled, too.

I played one of them: a new version of Meta’s classic VR-lightsaber fitness game Beat Saber called Beat Saber Flux, which is arriving next year to time with the glasses. Flux has no sabers at all, actually. Instead, the game tracked my hands as I formed energy fields to punch and slice through oncoming waves of targets. It reminded me more of rhythm games like Synth Riders and Supernatural, but also was a good demo of the headset’s hand tracking chops.

Meta’s VR Glasses wowed me with their size.Scott Stein/CNET

I also tried casting multiple virtual monitors in front of me from a wirelessly connected laptop, something you can already do on the Quest and headsets like the Vision Pro and Samsung’s Galaxy XR. But it’s the smaller size of the Meta VR Glasses that makes this achievement seem particularly impressive. 

I typed on a virtual keyboard projected directly onto the table in front of me, a trick Quest headsets can already do but which looked more impressive on Meta’s VR Glasses, particularly since the keyboard really looked as though it had been projected onto the table. It was properly positioned over my hands with realistic occlusion effects. But I don’t know how well it would work beyond my rapid hunt and pecking.

Another look at the glasses and their processor puck.Celso Bugatti/CNET

Navigating Meta’s hand and eye tracking interfaces felt fine, and again, very Apple Vision-esque. But also like Meta’s neural band hand gestures for its Ray-Ban Display glasses. Taps and thumb-swipes on my closed fist handled scrolling around, but I found that pinch-and-pull gestures in the air worked for scrolling too. It wasn’t always that easy to make out on-screen indicators of where my eyes were looking, though: Sometimes icons got a little bigger or wiggled, but not always.

Meta promises a 3-hour battery life with the included processor puck, which can fast recharge at 45W. It runs off a Qualcomm Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset, the same one that’s in Xreal’s upcoming processor puck-tethered, VR-like pair of Android XR glasses, Xreal Aura.

Meta’s VR Glasses are small but they pack impressive micro OLED displays inside.Scott Stein/CNET

A clear display upgrade

In a half-hour demo session at Meta’s Connect developer conference, I watched a series of movie clips and videos meant to show off the quality of the headset as a portable cinema. The twin micro OLED displays with a combined effective 5K resolution felt as vivid as that of a Vision Pro, to my memory, but with a smaller 84-degree field of view. They’re 2,412×2,288 pixels per eye.

Watching a few movies on the Meta VR Glasses looked better than anything I’ve seen on Quest headsets, and clearly offers a step-up to approach the good-enough-for-home-cinema feel I get in the Vision Pro.

Beat Saber Flux is a hand tracking-focused game update for Meta VR Glasses (and coming to Quest too). Meta

Meta’s promising lots of streaming video app support. I viewed a series of brief Disney interactive environments for some of its streaming movies, which tried to give me a taste of something more immersive than what’s already on the Vision Pro and Quest’s Disney Plus app. As I watched Avengers: Infinity War, my room was engulfed by parts of the stellar forge Nidavellir while a scene between Thor and Peter Dinklage’s dwarf king Eitri played on a big virtual movie screen. At one point, Groot also popped out in 3D beyond the screen’s dimensions.

The displays and spatial audio are Dolby Atmos and Dolby Vision capable, and Meta’s touting that the headset is certified for Imax film viewing in the proper aspect ratio. Meta’s launching its own movie store with these VR glasses, and it’ll also be available on Quest headsets.

In a sense, the Meta VR Glasses almost remind me of smaller micro OLED-equipped display glasses like the ones made by Viture and Xreal. They especially resemble Xreal’s upcoming Aura glasses, which I’ve tried several times and run Google’s Android XR operating system and connect to a processing puck. Aura’s field of view is even smaller at 70 degrees, but it’s more like a pair of display glasses that are remarkably VR-like. Meta’s headset feels like a VR headset that’s remarkably glasses-like. The two sort of meet in the middle.

This is how my early version of Hologram looks on a phone screen. It’s even more impressive in VR.Scott Stein/CNET

Holograms for chat, at last

A demo I tried in a separate session showed me something Meta’s been promising for years: realistic 3D avatars for video chat, much like what Apple already has in its Vision Pro Personas. Meta showed me early prototypes of its “Codec Avatar” vision for hyper-real avatar embodiment back in 2022 at its research labs, but the new Holograms feel like a slice of that, aimed at working on both VR Glasses, Quest headsets, and even Meta’s Ray-Ban Displays in its smaller 2D screen.

I was actually blown away by my Holograms demo, because what I saw didn’t look like uncannily real people: they looked exactly like real people, as if appearing in a video chat in front of me. A quick head scan and recording of my voice and expressions (mostly with smiling or positive emotions expressed) on a phone app led to a 3D scan of myself that then appeared inside VR Glasses when I made a WhatsApp call to a Meta team member. I couldn’t see myself, but I did see them appear in front of me, first as a 3D torso in a window, then opening out to stand in the room with me, legs and all, when I tapped an icon in my chat window.

It looked like a volumetric video capture of someone, not an artificial scan. And while Holograms currently animate body movement using AI to interpret voice tone, they’ll eventually have body tracking using the VR Glasses’ downward-facing cameras, which track both face and body movements. It seemed like they were in the room, right by a table in front of me…but turning in a ghostly manner to keep facing me no matter which way I turned.

Holograms are going to launch alongside Meta VR Glasses, but also get tested as a Met Ray-Ban Display feature in beta later this year for WhatsApp calling. The technology leans heavily on cloud compute, using stable diffusion versus Gaussian splatting like Apple’s Personas uses. I’ve never seen a more realistic deepfaked version of myself before.

The Meta Ray-Ban Gen 3 glasses (left) next to Meta VR Glasses (right). They’re getting closer in size than ever.Scott Stein/CNET

The start of a new phase for VR and AR?

My time with the Meta VR Glasses impressed me, especially compared to other recent VR devices and display glasses I’ve tried, and I immediately thought about what it would be like to travel with them. But their unusual design and higher price, clearly aimed at making a premium experience for movie-watching, immersive HD video and wearable displays, is a risk. It’s a play that Meta hasn’t made since the Quest Pro was released back in 2022.

Would I use the Meta VR Glasses for work? Maybe. I like that they can also connect directly to a laptop, phone or any other UBS-C device with video out to turn them into a portable display, but Xreal Aura will do that too. I also like that they’ll run all the Quest apps I already use, but Meta’s still facing an uphill battle over all the Android and iOS apps Google and Apple’s XR devices can tap into. 

How long will it be until Meta’s VR and glasses lines converge?Scott Stein/CNET

I feel more comfortable with Meta as a wear-sometimes device maker in the VR space. I’m much less happy with Meta as a broker of some sort of always-on glasses-based personal assistant (which is where all the AI glasses are headed). But, clearly, those categories are merging, slowly. The VR Glasses feel like an early herald of the attempted merge.

Which raises my final question: Are the Meta VR Glasses a premium upgrade for Quest owners, a portable upsell or a pitch to reach people who’ve never tried VR or AR before? I definitely found them more wearable than any Quest headset, with no pressure on my face and a more casual comfort. 

I kept thinking about Valve’s recently released Steam Frame, a headset that costs a similar amount but has a more traditional but modular VR headset design. Valve’s Frame wants to push Steam into new forms. Meta’s VR Glasses are aiming to push the Quest library into new forms, too. And then there are Xreal’s similar Aura glasses coming this fall, and even Snap Specs, which are full augmented reality glasses with clear lenses but have no processor puck tether at all.

They all want to come with me on a trip. Which would I actually take? Or afford? Meta VR Glasses aren’t even on sale until next spring, but I’m already wondering if they’ll be something I’d pick over alternatives, or whether Meta’s VR glasses flex is more of a stepping stone to AR glasses the company can’t quite make happen yet. But I want another go in them, for sure. And I’d love to travel with them next year.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Scott Stein
						

						

							Editor at Large						
					

											

								

											I started with CNET reviewing laptops in 2009. Now I explore wearable tech, VR/AR, tablets, gaming and future/emerging trends in our changing world. Other obsessions include magic, immersive theater, puzzles, board games, cooking, improv and the New York Jets. title: Disney+ starts rolling out another price hike, no ad plans starting at $21.49/month
snippet: Yet another price hike is imminent for Disney+ and Hulu, with the new plans going up by around $2 per month. more…
fullText:
Yet another price hike is imminent for Disney+ and Hulu, with the new plans going up by around $2 per month.

Bloomberg first reported on the incoming price hike, which is said to kick in today. While Disney+’s website and documentation still show existing pricing for us, our sister site 9to5Mac did see the updated pricing already live.

title: New iPad mini coming soon with these major changes
snippet: Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month. more…
fullText:
Apple is about to release a new iPad mini. This will mark the first update to the device in two years, and it’s expected to be a big one. Here’s everything we know so far about the new iPad mini coming as soon as next month.

OLED display

By far the biggest change to the new iPad mini will be to the display. According to multiple sources, the iPad mini 8 will feature an OLED display.

This will be a dramatic improvement to the iPad mini’s current LCD panel. For users, the move to OLED means deeper blacks, richer colors, and better contrast. The iPhone X was the first iPhone to use an OLED display in 2017, while the OLED iPad Pro debuted in 2024.

One lingering question, though, is whether the new iPad mini will use a ProMotion display for refresh rates of up to 120Hz. According to a sketchy rumor last week, the new iPad mini won’t offer ProMotion support and will instead be limited to 60Hz.

This hasn’t been corroborated by any other sources, though, so I’m holding out hope this leak is incorrect.

New chip

The current iPad mini, released in October 2024, is powered by Apple’s A17 Pro chip. The new iPad mini will likely feature the A19 Pro or A20 Pro chip. This will offer a solid boost in performance, and could enable support for the most advanced Siri AI features in iOS 27.

Better water resistance

According to Bloomberg, Apple has tested a “redesigned casing” for the iPad mini that is water-resistant like the iPhone.

Whether or not this water-resistant casing pans out remains to be seen. However, it would make the iPad mini far more durable. It’d be especially notable for people who use it as an e-reader, as one of the top features of dedicated e-readers like the Kindle is water resistance.

New speaker technology

The iPad mini 8 might also be Apple’s first device with a revamped vibration-based speaker system. This vibration-based speaker system would let Apple remove speaker holes, aiding its work to make the device water-resistant.

In contrast, the iPhone has speaker holes, but Apple uses gaskets and adhesives to make the device water-resistant.

New iPad mini release date

According to the latest reporting from Bloomberg, Apple is aiming to release the OLED iPad mini as early as this October. It’s allegedly the “biggest overhaul to the iPad mini in half a decade.”

There’s no word on how much the new iPad mini will cost. Apple increased the price of the current iPad mini in July from $499 to $599 (currently discounted to $569 on Amazon). Whether the new iPad mini with OLED is even more expensive remains to be seen.

What do you think of Apple’s rumored plans for the iPad mini? Are you tempted by the OLED display? Let us know down in the comments.

snippet: Google is reportedly nearing the launch of its long awaited Gemini 4 model, after dawdling behind rival developers on flagship AI releases. fullText:
Jess Weatherbed

 

is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.

Google is reportedly nearing the launch of its long awaited Gemini 4 model, after dawdling behind rival developers on flagship AI releases. Speaking with The Information during his first media appearance as the leader of Google’s DeepMind division, Koray Kavukcuoglu said that Gemini 4 is currently in its refinement stage, and that the company is aiming to launch the model “much earlier” than the end of the year.

“Our intention is to, like — as soon as possible — to release an early post-training output because we see the results and we are excited,” Kavukcuoglu told the publication, adding that Google would “continue the fast-paced iterations” going forward. This hopefully marks Google returning to a more consistent AI release timeline following a shakeup at DeepMind’s top leadership, with former AI head Demis Hassabis stepping down in August after announcing that “great progress” was being made on Gemini 4.

Google hasn’t released a new flagship AI model since the Gemini 3 series in November 2025. OpenAI’s GPT-6 and Anthropic’s Mythos series models have launched since then. Both outperform Gemini 3 and give the rival AI providers a sizable lead against Google in the AI race. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said at the I/O event in May that a major Gemini 3.5 Pro update would be coming in June to help bridge the gap, but the model was never rolled out.

Kavukcuoglu said the company “took a little bit of a step back” to focus on introducing faster, less powerful Flash models instead of releasing Gemini 3.5 Pro. When asked whether he was concerned about Google falling behind its rivals on AI development, he told The Information that “In my mind, it’s a certainty that we are always gonna be at the frontier.”
