title: Apple didn’t give up on stylus support for iPhone Duo; Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold should take notes
snippet: Apple’s iPhone Duo may not have reinvented the Android foldable, but it certainly did put a polish on a number of things. Inlcuded in that list is stylus support on the iPhone Duo, something that was more complicated behind-the-scenes than it initially sounded like, and an effort that Samsung should probably take note of. more…
fullText:
Apple’s iPhone Duo may not have reinvented the Android foldable, but it certainly did put a polish on a number of things. Inlcuded in that list is stylus support on the iPhone Duo, something that was more complicated behind-the-scenes than it initially sounded like, and an effort that Samsung should probably take note of.

Rewinding, Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold series first added stylus support back in 2022 on the Galaxy Z Fold 3. Samsung made a special version of the S Pen stylus for foldables that didn’t require a battery, but also didn’t stow away inside of the foldable. Still, it was fully supported and a welcome tool, especially as the Galaxy Note series was dying off. But with last year’s Galaxy Z Fold 7, Samsung ditched support for the S Pen in order to make the foldable much thinner.

S Pen support on Galaxy Z Fold 4 and Fold 5

But, of course, Samsung is likely rethinking that decision now that Apple has introduced the iPhone Duo with stylus support.

Apple touts that the iPhone Duo will support the USB-C version of the Apple Pencil that’s otherwise made for iPads. It sounds simple enough, but there’s more to the story. Bloomberg reports that Apple originally wanted to make a dedicated version of Apple Pencil for the iPhone Duo, a version that would have been shorter and able to magnetically hold itself on the Duo’s hinge. 

	

That stylus wasn’t announced as, apparently, Apple ran into “technical problems ahead of mass production” a few months before the Duo was announced, leading to the pivot over to iPad versions of the stylus. The report further notes that Apple’s software update to enable this isn’t “as simple as hitting a button” and that it won’t arrive until “fairly late in 2026.” 

Still, that’s more than Samsung is bringing to the table at this point. Both the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra lack any support for a stylus, despite rumors of Samsung exploring other ways of offering a stylus on its foldables. The reason the traditional S Pen doesn’t work in these thin form factors is that it requires a physical layer in the display assembly and, as such, adds to the thickness and weight – two pillars that Samsung is hyper-focused on improving with each generation. 

Samsung’s Android competition has embraced stylus support, so between that and Apple’s adoption (mostly the latter, obviously), it’s all the more likely Galaxy Z Fold 9 will bring stylus support page in one form or another. Samsung has left the door open, too.

fullText:
If you’re anything like me, you’ve been all-in on smart lights for years. I almost never use light switches anymore and the luxury I’ve grown used to is immediately made apparent when I spend a night away from home. That said, smart lighting has continued to evolve far beyond the basic bulbs I’ve grown used to, and this was plain as day when I got my hands on the new Linkind Smart Light Stick.

First and foremost, these bulbs pack Matter compatibility for simple controls, but the perks really come to life when you tap into the AiDot app. This is where you can take advantage of addressable zones within the bulb, which sort of blew my mind. I also love the clean cylindrical look of these bulbs, which I will showcase down below.

The first thing that stood out to me when unboxing it was the hardware design. Rather than sticking to the familiar pear shape of standard household bulbs, Linkind opted for a clean, frosted cylinder. For this reason, I really think it will look great in frosted and transparent fixtures alike.

Matter-compatible bulbs with rich app customization

The setup process was refreshingly straightforward. As shown in the screenshots, grabbing the AiDot app and running through the pairing sequence took about a minute or so, and I was relieved straight away when I saw that the app actually had solid ratings. While Matter certification allows users to skip third-party apps entirely, skipping AiDot would cause you to miss out on a lot of the features that an app like AiDot can offer.

	

As you can see below, the number of available scenes is sort of obscene. It was a little overwhelming to see the number of options, but it’s easy to create favorites, which I’ll certainly be doing so it is easy to switch for whatever holiday season we are in the middle of.

To put these bulbs through their paces, I installed them across three different fixtures. First up was the pergola and hot tub area. Transparent wall mounted lanterns along the white lattice frame gave the Light Sticks plenty of room to show off. I then added them to one of the lamp posts in my yard, followed by the lamp that resides in my home office.

Hero feature is the customizable flame effect

Easily the coolest trick up the Light Stick’s sleeve is its built-in flame simulation. Rather than settling for a basic pixelated flicker, the frosted cylindrical design diffuses light to deliver a much more authentic look than I tend to see with other bulbs, especially when dropped into an open fixture like my office lamp or outdoor lanterns.

Setup is straight forward, allowing me to quickly customize the look I was after. I did my best to capture it in action in the video below. In my opinion, the video doesn’t quite do it justice, as I think it looks much better in person.

Seasonal curb appeal with festive scenes

Until now, I’ve been going with warm white lighting 100% of the time. With Linkind Smart Light Stick Pro, I don’t have a reason to forego shaking up the look of my space when the seasons change or a holiday arrives.

While there are plenty of pre-made dynamic scenes to pick from, the DIY tab in the AiDot app is where the hardware really shines. As mentioned earlier, there are individually addressable zones, offering up 50 individual areas you can customize. I was able to use the app to create a neat color effect in under a minute, and you can see the UI below.

The settings above lead to another neat animation that I tried to capture on video. Like before, while it looks great on video, it’s even better in person. I took the lamp shade off and you can see that the bulb looks great even when fully on display, which is something I cannot say for a lot of the other smart bulbs out there.

And if you want clearer examples of what the bulbs actually look like in person, check out the official footage in the video below. It highlights a wider variety of dynamic presets, from festive holiday scenes to subtle ambient glows. It really drives home just how versatile these are compared to standard, single-color smart bulbs.

Pricing and availability

If you want to step up your outdoor or indoor lighting like I have, head over to Linkind’s website to find these bulbs (and all of the others they sell). You can pick up the bulbs directly on Amazon, where they are currently selling for $39.99.

title: Meta’s next VR device isn’t a headset — it’s glasses
snippet: The Meta VR Glasses. | Photo by Brett Putman / The Verge Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket. The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at M … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Meta is launching new VR hardware: a pair of glasses. The new Meta VR Glasses sit on your ears like a typical pair of glasses instead of being strapped over your head, but they still have immersive displays for watching movies, playing games, and getting work done. Imagine a pair of hefty black sunglasses with blacked-out lenses on the outside, but the components of a typical VR headset distributed between the device on your head and a computing puck in your pocket.

The idea is to give you a way to experience VR in a much lighter and more approachable form factor than Vision Pro or Meta Quest-style headsets. I got to try the VR Glasses at Meta’s campus this week, and as Meta walked me through some familiar VR demos like watching content, playing a game, and working from multiple screens, I was impressed by how much lighter the whole experience felt. Some of that was about the literal weight, as the glasses come in at just 100g, far less than the Quest 3’s 515g. But there was also something lighter in a more intangible way: the glasses form factor made the headset seem like something I could easily jump in and out of instead of being a whole cumbersome commitment with big head straps. It felt like a lightweight Vision Pro, and is perhaps a better execution of some of what Apple wanted to do with that device.

To keep things light, the VR Glasses’ display and the sensors are all you actually wear on your face. The separate puck connected with a wire contains the guts powering the headset: a Snapdragon Reality Elite processor, 128GB of storage, 12GB of RAM, and the battery, which Meta says will offer up to three hours of media playback, though you can continue using the glasses even while the puck is being charged.

The display is what Meta calls a 5K MicroOLED “Infinite Display.” It has 2412 x 2288 pixels per eye at 37 pixels per degree and supports a refresh rate of up to 120Hz. On the front of the glasses are two cameras for color passthrough, letting you see through to the world around you. The headset comes in small and large sizes to offer different options for width, though they cost the same.

You primarily use your eyes and hand gestures to control the glasses. You just look at elements onscreen to navigate, and the OS will highlight what your eyes are looking at using two pairs of eye-tracking cameras. To select something that’s highlighted, you can pinch your thumb and pointer finger together, and to scroll around, you make a fist and move your thumb around the top of your hand. It feels similar to the gestures from the Meta Ray-Ban Display, but those require a neural wristband; the VR Glasses instead use six external cameras to follow your hands.

Based on my demos, I think the VR Glasses will be best for entertainment because of the big virtual screen. Meta showed me a clip from James Cameron’s Billie Eilish concert film, which was impressive on a huge virtual display, and parts of the most recent NBA Finals, which was filmed on a format called VR180 that provided a 180-degree view of the court. I also got to watch some of Avengers: Endgame in what Meta characterized as a “VR Enhanced Cinema” experience made in partnership with Disney and Industrial Light & Magic. In the entire VR environment around the screen showing the film, there were graphics that thematically lined up with what was actually happening onscreen that also changed as the clip went on; when a huge energy beam appeared at a major moment in the film featuring Thor, I saw one shoot out at the top of the VR environment, too. Meta says that VR enhanced versions of Avengers: Infinity War and Star Wars: A New Hope will be available when the VR Glasses launch.

Image: Meta

Gaming remains a major use case, too. Meta showed me a new mode for Beat Saber called Flux that supports playing with hands (though it will work with the Quest’s Touch Plus controllers, too). Instead of waving virtual sabers to hit blocks in time with the music, like in the original, Flux tasked me with moving my hands, which were each surrounded by balls of energy connected by pulsing electricity, to break through flying poles and smash targets. It makes sense when you play it, and the one song I played was really enjoyable. The VR Glasses will have more than 75 games at launch that will support the new hands-first experience (including a VR version of Phoenix Wright: Ace Attorney – Dual Destinies launching in 2027), but they’ll also support the entire current Quest app catalog and can connect to Touch Plus controllers (and Bluetooth controllers).

Meta is also pitching this as a way to browse apps and do some work, and I can see the vision. In one demo, I used the glasses to mirror three windows from a nearby laptop. You’ll be able to connect wirelessly to computers or other devices with a USB-C connection, which could be useful if you want more screen real estate for work. My favorite demo from my whole session was actually one about typing. While using a special version of Instagram made for the VR Glasses, I was prompted to leave a comment on a picture, but I was able to type that comment and navigate the app using a virtual keyboard and trackpad that appeared after I laid my hands flat on the table. To my surprise, the virtual keyboard and trackpad were actually good. Of course, the experience wasn’t as speedy as using a physical keyboard and mouse, but in a pinch for a short message or email, I think it could be quite useful. (I should note it’s not technically new; Meta introduced this for Quest headsets earlier this year, and I haven’t tried it on those devices.)

The glasses cost $1,299.99 and will go on sale in spring 2027. That price puts the VR Glasses between Meta’s $599.99 Quest 3 and a high-end VR headset like Apple’s $3,499 Vision Pro, and I think that’s the right way to think about them. I don’t think they will transform the landscape of VR, especially when Meta itself has been divesting from VR software and largely moving on from the VR version of Horizon Worlds.

Meta is still planning to develop full VR headsets, the company’s VP of product for VR, Angela Chang, tells The Verge. But as tech companies chase the next big hardware category, however, a new form factor is starting to emerge: something that’s more capable than most smart glasses but less overbearing than a full-on VR headset. Google and Xreal are teaming up on XR glasses. Snap’s idea is the augmented reality-focused Specs glasses, and Meta is working on AR glasses too. The VR Glasses represent another fascinating idea of what a computer on your head can be.

title: John Ternus just gave the best defense yet for Vision Pro
snippet: Apple’s new CEO John Ternus recently sat down for a lengthy, in-depth interview with French outlet Clique TV, and in it he gave the best defense yet for Apple Vision Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple’s new CEO John Ternus recently sat down for a lengthy, in-depth interview with French outlet Clique TV, and in it he gave the best defense yet for Apple Vision Pro.

John Ternus compares Vision Pro to the earliest days of personal computers

Apple Vision Pro is an oddity in Apple’s hardware lineup. It isn’t commercially successful the way the iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, and AirPods are. But the device is a technological marvel, and has garnered a small base of loyal fans who love it.

In the past, Tim Cook defended Vision Pro’s underwhelming sales by saying it’s an “early adopter product.”

Now John Ternus has weighed in, and I found his answer a more satisfying reason for Vision Pro to exist.

In a new interview, Clique TV’s Mouloud Achour asked Ternus: “The Vision Pro: for you is it a test, a flop, or the first step to the future of what’s going to be…a computer?”

Here’s what Ternus said:

Vision Pro to me is an amazing device. It’s an absolutely amazing device. But I think of it as like the early days of computers. It is the early days of a long journey. That’s how I feel about Vision Pro. What you see, if you think about the early days, people found different reasons where the computer allowed them, the Mac allowed them to do something never before possible. Like desktop publishing, and it became a big thing in that industry. 

What you’re seeing with Vision Pro now is, certainly there’s early adopters who love it and they’re using it and they’re enjoying it, but you also—surgeons are starting to use it in surgery because it’s just a fundamentally better tool for them than a monitor that’s kind of sitting over here. And so it’s growing in that area. In film production people are using it for set development and things like that. So we’re going to continue to grow and find more and more compelling use cases. And I think there’s a very bright future.

Ternus invokes Cook’s language of citing early adopters, but his comparison to the early days of computing is also helpful.

	

When personal computers first came on the scene, they were very expensive and had extremely limited use cases. But over time that changed, eventually unlocking possibilities that could scarcely have been imagined in the early days.

The dream of lightweight glasses offering full-fledged “spatial computing” features may be several years away. But it’s easy to see that future coming true, and the Vision Pro being a key part of that.

title: Pixel VIPs 2.0 redesign starts rolling out with fullscreen look
snippet: Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Feature Drop, Pixel VIPs 2.0 is beginning to roll out, and it brings more changes than just the widget redesign.

With version 2.0, tapping on a contact in the widget no longer slides up a bottom sheet over your homescreen. Instead, it now opens a fullscreen layout, which was previously accessible by swiping up. The previous design was better for one-handed use as the call and message shortcuts were closer to the bottom of the screen.

Other changes to this page include a pencil icon in the top-right corner that lets you quickly edit in Google Contacts, while the call, message, video, and contact buttons now use outline-style icons.

Old vs. new

	

Google has moved the “Local updates” card to the top spot over “Last connection,” while “Notes” is now the last section as Pixel VIPs has removed the media and place recommendations.

Meanwhile, the big update today is a new pill-shaped switcher that shows all your VIPs. This allows for quick switching without having to go back to the homescreen.

The actual widget redesign is not yet live after updating to Pixel VIPs 2.0. However, there is a preview of the new layout with “space for quick actions” that lets you call and message directly from the widget.

Pixel VIPs 2.0 is widely rolled out via the Play Store.

title: New Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 fitness feature is surprisingly motivating
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 include a new fitness-tracking feature: live step tracking on the watch face. Alongside live heart rate data, it’s a surprisingly welcome and motivating change to the new hardware that I’m loving so far.

Conceptually, step tracking data on the watch face is a rather unremarkable feature. Third-party apps like Pedometer++ have long been able to display your step count on your watch face. But Apple has waited until Series 12 and Ultra 4 to build in support for the Apple Watch.

Step tracking data has always been collected by Apple Watch. Even your iPhone can measure step tracking throughout the day, dating back to the iPhone 5s (before the Apple Watch existed). 

Before Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, however, Apple tucked step tracking data away inside apps like Fitness and Health. Now, it’s a built-in complication option from the Fitness app, just like activity rings. 

My guess is that Apple didn’t surface this data before for a two reasons. First, Apple’s new hardware is more capable and more efficient. That must be the reason why live step data is hardware-specific.

Second, I think Apple has liked the idea of presenting the Apple Watch as more comprehensive than just step tracking. The heart rate monitor and other sensors tell a much more complete story than just steps walked per day.

Whatever the thinking may have been before, we now have built-in live step tracking on the Apple Watch face. And the result? For me at least, it’s a surprisingly motivating number to view so far.

While I most appreciate live heart rate data for real-time insight, I’m finding that little step tracking number to be most beneficial when I start my day. It’s basically a race to get out of the hundreds and into the thousands. Otherwise that triple-digit number is just staring me down all day. 

My current strategy is to knock out a 16-minute rolling hills workout on my GymKit-equipped BowFlex T6 treadmill early in the day. This adjusts incline up and down, allowing me to focus on speed and a fixed session time. The sooner I knock out the mile run, the more time for a cooldown walk afterwards.

It’s also just really satisfying to watch the number increase as you walk, even if you’re not logging a workout. It’s a small thing, but it’s a welcome new way to gamify increasing your activity, especially if you’re anchored to a desk for much of the day.

title: Googlebook OS hands-on: It’s Android, stupid
snippet: An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks. more…
fullText:
An overwhelming sense of familiarity struck me the first time I used a Googlebook. That was immediately followed by a realization that this is just Android, and I think that feeling of similarity will go a long way in justifying and ultimately selling Googlebooks.

Going into this event, I was not particularly asking for a desktop operating system that felt like my Pixel phone. In fact, having used Chromebooks for many years (my first unit was the 2013 Acer C720), I thought Googlebook OS would not feel too different from ChromeOS. The desktop and app dock look the same, but the changes made by building on top of Android make all the difference.

That shared design and user experience allowed me to immediately start using Googlebook OS like a near-expert. Quick Settings and Notifications were obviously in the top-right corner, matching Android’s conventions. It’s a small change compared to ChromeOS, but it felt natural the first time I used it. I knew immediately to move the cursor to that top corner instead of the usual bottom corner on Chromebooks.

I also knew I could add and edit widgets, a long-requested feature ChromeOS lacks, by long-pressing on the desktop, while seeing the same ones from my phone homescreen evoked an almost nostalgia-like feeling.

	

The Settings app is identical to that on Pixel phones, while I was very happy to find Pixel Weather (and its widgets) along with the excellent Recorder pre-installed. Meanwhile, the app drawer is basically the Pixel Launcher. Compared to ChromeOS, you can put apps, widgets, and files/folders on the desktop for an infinite boost to productivity.

The best of the web 

Given how much Googlebook OS felt like using my Pixel phone, it was surprising to see that launching Gmail and Google Calendar opened the web versions rather than the Android apps. Talking with Google, I later learned that these were Trusted Web Activities (TWAs) instead of PWAs. Distributed from the Play Store, their main advantage is how this web wrapper-esque format allows for homescreen widgets.  

Zooming out, what shocked me was how much Googlebook OS leverages web apps, a move that strongly affirms the ChromeOS lineage. Going in, I assumed there would be a resurgence in desktop-class Android apps. 

However, I am told this was an intentional choice. Google’s viewpoint is ultimately to let app developers decide what the best strategy is for their application, and I think that’s fair. Google offered me the example of how it approached the Gmail and Workspace teams about whether they wanted to offer Googlebook adopters the web version or the Android app. They chose the former and ideally did not want to offer the Android app as an available Play Store download.

However, I do think this is partially a missed opportunity. Giving third-party developers a choice does reduce the barrier to entry for a new OS, but I strongly think Google internally should have enforced a strict first-party mandate to create desktop-class applications. 

Meanwhile, as I complained about in my Pixel Tablet review three years ago, it’s unbelievable that Google Messages is still using the same web-based version rather than anything more native. 

The Chrome browser on Googlebooks feels great and offers a full-featured experience from extensions to the new vertical tab list.

For all Android, always

That said, other experiences are clearly Android-powered. This includes the Google app and Gemini. When you invoke the Magic Pointer overlay, prompt responses appear in the Android Gemini app.

More broadly, Google sees this Android-based OS as an opportunity to leverage the existing Gemini and AI work done for phones as a starting point for the desktop. This is compared to having to rebuild everything from scratch for ChromeOS.

The on-device AI model is Gemini Nano, and that’s used to power AI descriptions of your screenshots that unlock search, as well as Magic Pointer, Rambler, and Create My Widget via a hybrid intelligence architecture.

I have to use the much-derided Magic Pointer a bit more to determine whether it’s some groundbreaking UX paradigm, but I do credit it for being very easy to enable. You will not forget that this feature exists on Googlebooks, and I think that could be valuable.

Rambler is the other major Gemini Intelligence feature, and you launch it from a Quick Insert key that’s in place of Caps Lock. Pressing the new Quick Insert key launches a rather convenient floating window that provides quick access to emoji, recent screenshots, and the Gboard clipboard, with Rambler in the bottom-right corner. This is a rather smart carryover from ChromeOS, now accessible with a single key press rather than a three-key combo.

Create My Widget is the other major tentpole. This is the introduction of generative UI to Android, and I think the ramifications for the future are tremendous. Right now, you get to make widgets that pull from live data sources, like Search. Googlebooks will definitely have to guide people on how to use this capability, but I think this could be a powerful selling point.

Google is adopting the successful Android OEM model for Googlebooks. However, they’ve fortunately drawn a line on how updates will work. Google is responsible for rolling out Googlebook OS updates, not OEMs, carrying over one of the strongest elements of ChromeOS. Partners will be able to specify preloaded apps, but they can’t do any heavy customization like altering what the status bar icons look like. The experience of using a Googlebook will be universal across partners. 

	

Google will be releasing major Googlebook OS updates on a quarterly basis to match the Android Quarterly Platform Release (QPR) model, but security updates can come at any time in between. 

Closing

Google spent a long time developing Googlebooks, and it shows. The specific example that really surprised me is that Google built an Antigravity app with native UI for Android. Going in, I thought they would just offer the Linux version, but this Antigravity for Android is distributed via the Play Store and interacts with the Linux terminal environment on Googlebook OS.

Frankly, Google fumbled its initial unveiling of Googlebooks in May. It was officially intended only as a preview, but the decision to highlight only a handful of features, including Magic Pointer, ended up being a great disservice. Googlebook OS is so much more than that, and the company should have led with the Android nature right off the bat.

Again, we actually have to see if it works in our daily workflows, but my initial impression is that Android gives Googlebooks a very solid foundation.

title: Here’s everything new for Apple Calendar in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with new features for Apple Wallet, Messages, Notes, and other system apps—including Calendar. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with new features for Apple Wallet, Messages, Notes, and other system apps—including Calendar. Here’s everything new for Apple’s Calendar app in iOS 27.

Natural language input for events and reminders

Calendar adds a feature in iOS 27 that’s been on my wishlist for years: natural language input.

Apple calls this ‘Smart Event Details,’ and it’s powered by Apple Intelligence. Here’s how it’s described:

Type events in your own words. Apple Intelligence fills in the title, time, location, and invitees as you go.

This works for both events and reminders. You can type in natural language when creating or editing an event, and watch the event details automatically fill in based on what you type.

If you prefer the manual approach, you can toggle this off in Settings, but I’ve been very happy to have it.

Design updates

Apple has updated Calendar’s design in iOS 27 in two main places:

Event details view

Event creation and editing

When you tap an event, it now pops up in a card overlay with a fresh design. Event options have been reorganized and given icons to make them visually pop.

And for event creation and editing, iOS 27 has an updated look too. Like with event details, Apple has reorganized the various options and added icons for each category.

Show as Busy/Free option for iCloud calendars

With modern digital calendars, the ability to mark yourself as busy or free related to a given event is a pretty standard feature. But until iOS 27, that option never existed for iCloud calendars.

If you use a Google calendar inside Apple’s app, you’ll see the event option to show yourself as busy or free. But for iCloud calendars, that’s long been missing.

iOS 27 finally remedies the oversight, offering a free/busy option for iCloud events like you would get for events from Google and other third-party calendar providers.

iOS 27 lets you make Home Screen and Today widgets bigger than ever thanks to a new extra-large size. And Calendar supports two extra-large widgets.

You can set up ’List’ and ‘Up Next’ widgets in the extra-large size. Each is great for showing more events and reminders than ever, so if you have a packed calendar, the new widgets could prove useful.

Extra-large widgets take up a lot of screen real estate, but they should prove especially handy on the iPhone Duo’s extra-large display.

Siri AI upgrades

It’s worth mentioning that Siri AI comes with plenty of upgrades relevant to the Calendar app.

Siri gains onscreen awareness, understands your personal context, and is overall more intelligent and capable than ever before. That means it’s a much better tool for managing your calendar. In my use of iOS 27, I’ve found myself relying much more on Siri for handling events and reminders.

There’s also a new visual intelligence button in the event creation screen that lets you scan an event flyer with the new Siri mode in the Camera app. Siri then creates a new event with the details.

title: Former Apple retail chief’s new ‘Shop Different’ book now available
snippet: Ron Johnson, Apple’s former senior vice president of retail operations, is out with a new book today called ‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius.’ In the book, Johnson tells the story of working alongside Steve Jobs to craft Apple’s retail strategy. more…
fullText:
Ron Johnson, Apple’s former senior vice president of retail operations, is out with a new book today called ‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius.’

In the book, Johnson tells the story of working alongside Steve Jobs to craft Apple’s retail strategy.

‘Shop Different,’ written with Zander Nethercutt, isn’t a “traditional business book,” but rather an “insider account of one of the most important retail successes of our time.”

Here’s the description:

When Steve Jobs hired Ron Johnson to create the Apple Store in 2000, con­ventional wisdom said that the inter­net would put stores out of business. By the time he left Apple in 2011, Johnson and his team had created the most respected and profitable retail stores in the world. And even then, skeptics were still predicting the death of physical retail.

In Shop Different, Johnson reveals how it happened: how he earned Jobs’s trust, how they developed a vision for a store that would win not by selling but by serving, and how he convinced Jobs that the store’s service philosophy should be rooted in some­thing as intangible as love. Johnson then gives readers a new look at Apple’s ascent to the most valuable company in the world; offers an inspiring vision for a future in which retailers win on connection, service, and experience; and shares an honest look at what leads to success—and what can follow.

Johnson joined 9to5Mac’s Overtime podcast last week to discuss ‘Shop Different’ and the origins of the Apple Store. Jeff and Fernando did an excellent job interviewing Johnson, and you can watch it on YouTube, or listen via Apple Podcasts and other platforms.

‘Shop Different: How Retail Revealed Apple’s Genius’ can be ordered on Amazon today. You can also order it and support local bookstores via Bookshop.org. My copy arrives today and I’m looking forward to diving in.

title: Gemini app for macOS adding send and read iMessage integration
snippet: Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week. more…
fullText:
Google’s latest update to the Gemini app for macOS readies local iMessage integration. This follows the app coming to Windows last week.

Gemini’s latest Connected App on the Mac is @messages to “Read, search, and send messages in Apple Messages.” Specifically, the integration can:

Send messages to contacts or phone numbers

Read recent conversations, unread messages, and search message history

This will aid context by being able to look up information from conversations. Example prompts include:

Send a message to John: “Running 5 minutes late!”

Show my recent messages from Sarah

Search Messages for dinner reservations

 In terms of limitations, Gemini cannot:

	

Manage group participant membership or change group chat photos

Schedule messages for future delivery or edit sent messages

Send file, photo, or media attachments (plain text messages only)

Send tapback reactions (love, like, dislike, laugh, emphasize, question)

Generate photos or images within automated task workflows

This integration appears in Settings > Connected Apps at the very bottom after updating to version 1.116.5.889 of Gemini for macOS. However, as of this afternoon, a server-side component appears to be missing, with @messages not yet recognized in the prompt box.

Recent updates to Gemini for macOS introduced a File Providers extension that shows “Add to Gemini” when you right-click on a file in Finder. This immediately adds the photo or document to the prompt box. It can be enabled in Settings > Extensions. Google also added Images, Videos, and Daily Brief to the side panel.

fullText:
New images of a Googlebook laptop from Asus have surfaced, showing off of selection of ports and a big ol’ trackpad.

We first caught a glimpse at Asus’ Googlebook last month, and now new images offer a closer look at what Asus is bringing to the table. The Mac Observer obtained a batch of images with a few more angles.

Based on side views of the machine, it looks like there are at least two USB-C ports, a couple of USB-A ports, and a headphone jack. The keyboard doesn’t look particularly shallow, there’s a fingerprint sensor, and the trackpad looks pretty huge. There’s also a lightbar on the outside and the display extends pretty closely to each corner. 

Other images showcase a dedicated “G” key around where the Start button shows on a Windows machine, or CMD on a MacBook, while there’s also a fan in this particular model.

title: Delayed Apple TV series ‘The Savant’ may finally air next year
snippet: If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date … more…
fullText:
If you cast your mind back to almost a year ago from today, Apple TV was about to launch a new series called The Savant starring Jessica Chastain … until it was pulled from the schedule at the last moment, in the wake of the assassination of political activist Charlie Kirk. 

Apple never gave an exact reason for cancelling the release, but promised it would release the series at a later date …

At the time, star Jessica Chastain made a statement to say that she was ‘not aligned’ with Apple’s decision to postpone the show’s premiere.

Nevertheless, here we are a year later, and The Savant has still not come out. In fact, if you look up the series in the Apple TV app, the page still reads “coming at a later date” and has an awkwardly outdated ‘2025’ year label. 

However, Variety reports today that the streamer has finally put the series back on its slate, with a release date scheduled for spring 2027.

The spring launch would aim to put the series in prime contention for the next Emmy awards season, which means Apple would want to get all episodes aired sometime before the cutoff date of May 31, 2027.

Of course, Apple could decide to once again delay the release when we get closer to springtime. Whatever Chastain’s thoughts are on how The Savant has been handled, the actress has continued to work with Apple on other upcoming projects, including starring in ‘The Dealer’ with Adam Driver, and alongside Ben Stiller in ‘The Off Weeks’.

title: iFixit tears down iPhone 18 Pro, explores variable aperture, finds concerning repair issue
snippet: iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below. more…
fullText:
iFixit has published its traditional teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro, which shows the variable aperture mechanism up close and explores a potential issue involving display repairs. Watch it below.

iFixit worries about possible display frame issue

iFixit’s teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro is now live, exploring not just the variable aperture, this year’s biggest camera upgrade, but also the device’s larger vapor chamber, the new under-display Face ID camera, and more.

When it comes to the variable aperture mechanism, iFixit notes that its six tiny blades are controlled by electromagnets, much like the optical image stabilization system, though the two mechanisms operate independently.

During the teardown, one of the tiny aperture blades flew out as iFixit dismantled the lens stack, underscoring how impractical a component-level repair would be. The group says that if the aperture gets stuck, it would likely require replacing the entire main camera assembly.

Another highlight of the new iPhone 18 Pro is its under-display Face ID infrared camera. For this year’s Pro devices, Apple moved the infrared camera beneath the display, while keeping the selfie camera and IR dot projector within the smaller Dynamic Island.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that Apple hides the relocated infrared camera by removing every other row of pixels above the sensor. iFixit notes that the effect fades toward the edges, and that there is an IR-pass filter beneath the OLED layer to block visible light.

Interestingly, the filter doesn’t extend all the way to the edge of the opening, creating what iFixit describes as an “eclipse effect” under certain microscope settings.

As for the iPhone 18 Pro’s bigger vapor chamber, the teardown offers a closer look at Apple’s redesigned cooling architecture.

As the company explained during its “Surprise and Shine” event, the A20 Pro uses a new package that places the silicon die side-by-side with the memory, removing the latter from the SoC’s thermal path and allowing the chip to connect directly to the vapor chamber. Apple also said the new vapor chamber has three times the surface area of the one in the iPhone 17 Pro.

iFixit’s teardown lets us see that setup up close, including the thermal material that presses the A20 Pro directly against the vapor chamber and the chamber itself extending across much of the phone’s body.

Now for the concerning part: iFixit says the plastic frame around the display was damaged on three of the four iPhones its team opened.

While the group notes that other iPhone 18 Pro teardowns haven’t encountered the same issue, and that Apple has been using this same plastic frame since the iPhone 15 Pro, it says it’s too early to tell whether this was an anomaly or a broader repairability concern.

iFixit also suggests that the device’s improved thermal system may be drawing heat away from the display as the heating pad tries to soften the adhesive.

Be that as it may, in practice, as iFixIt explains in the video, a cracked frame means the display may no longer sit perfectly flush after reassembly, and could compromise the phone’s water resistance.

Add to that the fact that some components remain difficult to reach, particularly the USB-C port, which iFixit says requires removing much of the phone’s internals to replace, and DIY repairs of the iPhone 18 Pro may prove challenging depending on which component needs replacing.

All in all, iFixit says the iPhone 18 Pro carries over many of the same repairability strengths and weaknesses as last year’s model, including the glue-free battery tray and modular camera assemblies, but also the need to enter through the display for most major repairs.

For now, the group has given both the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max a provisional repairability score of 7 out of 10 as it waits for parts, conducts more tests, and watches whether the display frame issue proves widespread.

title: Pixel Now Playing update brings interface tweaks & notifications [U]
snippet: The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks. more…
fullText:
The next wave of Pixel app updates is starting with Google rolling out the latest version of Now Playing with interface tweaks.

Update 9/17: Following a server-side update, Now Playing 2026.08.27x and Android System Intelligence C.6 reintroduces Recognized Music Notifications. These silent alerts let you see what’s playing without having to open the app or checking the Quick Settings Tile. Expanding the notification lets you jump to the History tab and favorite songs.

Enabled by default, you can disable them in Now Playing Settings > Notifications.

Original 9/2: When tapping on an identified song’s three-dot button, Now Playing slides up a bottom sheet. This replaces the floating menu and is better for one-handed navigation.

	

You’ll see track information with side-by-side buttons for Share, Add to favorites, and Remove from history. This is followed by a button to play the song and any shortcuts specific to your connected music service.

Meanwhile, the Favorites tab now includes dates and times like the History feed. There are also icon and spacing tweaks in Now Playing Settings.

The redesigned Now Playing launched in March, while Google in April reintroduced the “Tap to see what’s playing” shortcut on the lockscreen.

Version 2026.08.27.x of Pixel Now Playing is widely rolling out via the Google Play Store.

This follows last month’s updates to Pixel Journal that added more tools and Screenshots (extra filter options), as well as new icons for Google Calculator, Clock, Pixel Magnifier, Recorder, and Weather.

title: LinkedIn Adds More Profile Verifications to Combat AI-Powered Job Scams
snippet: Your coworkers and classmates can now vouch that you really do have a specific university or job on your resume.
fullText:
This news is not for people who like to lie on their resume. LinkedIn is adding new ways to verify where you work and went to school, the company announced on Wednesday. The new verifications for members and companies come amid a torrent of AI-powered scams wreaking havoc on social media platforms and the job market. Generative AI makes it easier to create fake media or impersonate specific people, like recruiters or executives.

“With advancements in AI, pretending to be someone that you’re not is getting increasingly cheaper and easier,” Oscar Rodriguez, vice president of LinkedIn’s trust products, told me in an interview. “And with that, authenticity is becoming increasingly important, perhaps more important than it has ever been.” As of September, more than 115 million of LinkedIn’s billion members have added verifications to their profiles. 

	

			

Individual LinkedIn members can verify their current workplace or university by getting two or more colleagues to vouch for them. You’ll need to have been connected to the person vouching for you for at least one year and have two-factor authentication enabled. You won’t be able to vouch for every single person you went to school with or in your office, but those limits are designed to ensure bad actors don’t take advantage of the tool.

Requests to verify your classmates and colleagues will appear under a new, separate section under My Network. LinkedIn says verified accounts see 50% more engagement on their posts and nearly 90% more profile views. 

And if you’re a page admin for a company page on LinkedIn, you can now also remove people falsely claiming to work at your company from LinkedIn’s search results. This is less about cutting down on clout chasers than it is about weeding out scammers who may falsely claim to be a recruiter or executive with a company in order to glean money and personal information from job hunters. Job scams are a growing problem; in a March 2026 survey from the cybersecurity firm Norton, 33% of US respondents said they had encountered a fake recruiter, phishing attempt or fraudulent job posting. Those who fell victim almost always lost money, nearly $9,000 each on average.

How to use LinkedIn’s verification tools

Verification on LinkedIn is free, but it’s a little bit different than other social media platforms. In addition to claiming a person is who they say they are, these tools can also verify where someone goes to school and works. 

Click the down arrow next to your profile picture in the upper-right menu. Click Settings & Privacy.

Click Verifications under Account.

Add verifications for your workplace, education and identity as prompted.

Once you do verify these things, people who view your LinkedIn profile will be prompted to view your verifications when their mouse hovers over your name. You’ll also get an icon that looks like a checkmark inside a shield next to your name. This is the badge you want to look for on company pages when you see a new job listing and get a message from someone claiming to be a recruiter. 

For more info on LinkedIn’s verification tools, check out this help page. You can also read more about LinkedIn’s new AI slop button.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2

Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. She graduated from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill with a degree in media and journalism. You can reach her at kchedraoui@cnet.com.

title: Gmail adds ‘Copy code’ shortcut for 2FA on Android & iOS
snippet: After rolling out Live search and chat earlier this month, Gmail now has a useful “Copy code” button for 2FA on Android and iOS. more…
fullText:
After rolling out Live search and chat earlier this month, Gmail now has a useful “Copy code” button for 2FA on Android and iOS.

Instead of having to open an email to select and copy the two-factor authentication code, Gmail now shows a shortcut directly in your inbox. The pill-shaped “Copy code 000000” button appears below the subject line, like the previews for images, documents, and other attachments.

Tapping the button simply adds the code to your clipboard for a quick paste in the designated app. 

We’ve seen it work for store and banking emails in our brief testing today. It’s a nice quality-of-life addition.

	

The Copy code button is appearing in Gmail for Android (version 2026.09.07.x) and iOS (6.0.260907), but not on the web. This shortcut would also be useful in email notifications on Android.

title: YouTube announces Custom Feeds, GIF comments, and ’Your podcast lineup’
snippet: At Made on YouTube 2026 today, YouTube announced a slew of new features. We’ve highlighted the capabilities that will impact the viewer experience over the coming months. more…
fullText:
At Made on YouTube 2026 today, YouTube announced a slew of new features. We’ve highlighted the capabilities that will impact the viewer experience over the coming months.

YouTube app

Custom Feeds will let you conversationally create a dedicated tab from the Homepage for “specific moods, routines, or your latest interests.” Multiple feeds can be created, with examples including “evening wind down with long documentaries” or “new DIY creators.” This feature is coming to US users on web, mobile, and TVs “soon.”

Ask YouTube is getting shopping features that let you “receive organized video recommendations, such as a comparison table that includes product attributes and categories based on your preferences.”

Once you click on a video that interests you most, you can continue asking more questions about the product directly on the video’s watch page.

This fall, YouTube comments will support GIFs. The mobile comment box will let you search a library of GIFs with this type of commenting available on videos and Shorts.

	

The in-app direct messaging feature is adding support for group chats. This is coming this fall in the US, UK, Singapore, Brazil, and some European countries.

YouTube Music + Podcasts

YouTube Music is getting a “personalized AI-audio guide” called Your podcast lineup. You get a “weekly spoken preview of recommended shows” that will dive into why you’ll like them. It then proceeds to suggested episodes, with this touted as being a “completely eyes-optional and hands-free” experience.

Meanwhile, the Ask Music chat found in the Home tab is getting new features that let you “customize your queue or dive deeper into artist lore.”

Both updates are “coming soon to YouTube Music and Premium subscribers worldwide.”

YouTube will stream Coachella through 2030. The 2027 edition will mark “15 years of bringing the desert festival experience to fans worldwide.”

YouTube Shorts 

YouTube is introducing a Shorts series feature that lets Creators organize their Shorts into seasons and episodes for a more structured and episodic experience. This is rolling out starting today. 

In a related development, the Shorts feed will start to recommend posts. Google shared that over 300 million users engage with Posts on YouTube every day. These text posts will also be coming to TVs in the “coming months.”

For YouTube Creators 

YouTube is piloting a Live auto-dubbing feature in early 2027 that “automatically translates your speech in real time” to let viewers “listen along in their preferred language as you speak.”

YouTube is testing “opt-in AI-powered comment moderation.” It will learn your “unique moderation style and needs over time.”
